# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Title: Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 initiates selective nuclear import failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in TDP-43-proteinopathy motor neurons.

Hypothesis statement. In vulnerable motor neurons of ALS characterized by TDP-43 proteinopathy (scoping to sporadic disease; C9orf72-initiated disease is intentionally excluded as a separate context), sustained cellular stress activates a nuclear kinase that phosphorylates the FG-repeat nucleoporin Nup98 at interphase sites. This phosphorylation weakens the NPC permeability barrier and Ran-dependent selective import - the initiating lesion. TDP-43 egress to the cytoplasm and transport-factor sequestration are downstream amplifiers, not the first cause.

Supported premises (from the packet only).
- S1: in ALS/FTD tissue and experimental systems, NPC components associate with insoluble TDP-43, and disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport. This establishes that pore/transport dysfunction accompanies TDP-43 pathology, but not its direction.
- S3: persistent, stress-granule-independent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies impair nuclear import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, recruit or mislocalize transport proteins, and are associated with cell death. This supports the downstream amplification arm.
- S4: stress granules sequester transport factors and impair transport; altering SG assembly modifies transport phenotypes. This defines the sequestration-based alternative my hypothesis must be discriminated from.
- S2: C9orf72 repeat RNA mislocalizes RanGAP and impairs import in patient-derived neurons. This supports transport dysfunction in that genetic context only; the hypothesis does not claim to cover it, though convergence is allowed.

Assumptions and speculative bridges (unverified by any supplied source).
- A1: an interphase kinase phosphorylates Nup98 in adult motor neurons. Candidate assumption: stress-activated p38/JNK; alternative assumption: ectopic mitotic-like kinase activity. No packet source supports any kinase.
- A2: the relevant phospho-sites cluster in or near Nup98 FG repeats and phosphorylation there raises passive permeability and lowers selective import. This is motivated by unverified prior knowledge that Nup98 is multiply phosphorylated during mitotic NPC disassembly - analogy only, not packet evidence.
- A3 (directional inversion): pore phosphorylation precedes TDP-43 egress. S1 documents co-occurrence, not direction.
- A4: the mechanism is specific to TDP-43-proteinopathy ALS rather than universal.

Causal chain. Initiating: stress kinase activation -> Nup98 phosphorylation -> weakening of the FG network -> passive leak plus selective import decline plus Ran-gradient dissipation -> failure to retain/import nuclear TDP-43. Downstream: cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing (S3-type, SG-independent), SG-mediated transport-factor sequestration (S4-type), further transport collapse, cell death.

Alternative explanations to discriminate.
1. Sequestration-first: SGs or TDP-43 assemblies deplete soluble import machinery; phosphorylation is absent or irrelevant.
2. Physical displacement: insoluble TDP-43 directly anchors to or distorts pores (consistent with S1), with phosphorylation as a bystander.
3. Genetic route: C9orf72 repeat RNA/DPR mechanisms (S2) produce the same transport phenotype independently.
4. Reverse causality: phosphorylation is a late consequence of stress or of pore disassembly, not an initiator.

Discriminating preclinical strategy (temporal plus perturbational).
- Models: isogenic human iPSC-derived motor neurons with TDP-43-proteinopathy phenotypes (sporadic patient lines; optionally inducible nuclear TDP-43 depletion) and healthy isogenic controls.
- Temporal test: time-resolved phosphoproteomics of purified nuclear-envelope fractions plus high-content imaging of phospho-Nup98 signal, NLS-reporter import, Ran-gradient integrity, and TDP-43 localization across stress onset. Hypothesis predicts the Nup98 phospho-signal rises before import declines and before TDP-43 egress; sequestration-first predicts soluble transport-factor depletion precedes any detectable Nup phosphorylation.
- Perturbational test: CRISPR knock-in of phospho-null (Ser/Thr to Ala) and phosphomimetic (Ser/Thr to Asp/Glu) Nup98 alleles. Support: phospho-null preserves import and nuclear TDP-43 even with stress granules assembling normally, and phosphomimetic Nup98 acutely impairs import in unstressed neurons without inducing TDP-43 aggregates. Contra-support: phospho-null fails to rescue while SG dissolution rescues transport with no Nup phospho-dependence.
- Kinase test: small-molecule blockade plus a conditional kinase-null allele; require concordant rescue to control off-targets; monitor SG formation in parallel so kinase effects on granules are not confounded with pore phosphorylation.
- Mechanistic separation: co-measure passive NPC permeability (small-tracer flux), facilitated import rates, and Ran gradient, distinguishing pore modification from transport-factor depletion rather than relying on timing alone.
- In vivo and tissue: neuron-targeted Nup98 phospho-site editing or kinase inhibition in a conditional TDP-43 mislocalization mouse model, with motor-neuron import markers, TDP-43 localization, and motor behavior/ survival as endpoints; post-mortem ALS motor cortex/spinal cord immunostained for phospho-Nup98 in neurons lacking cytoplasmic TDP-43 inclusions (early) versus affected neurons (late).

Falsifying observation. In phospho-null Nup98 knock-in stressed motor neurons, nuclear import still fails and TDP-43 still mislocalizes, while soluble transport factors are depleted from the nucleoplasm temporally before any detectable Nup98 phosphorylation; additionally, phosphomimetic Nup98 leaves import kinetics unchanged in healthy neurons. Both outcomes together would falsify the initiating-phosphorylation hypothesis.

Limitations. The hypothesis is scoped to TDP-43-proteinopathy ALS and may not generalize to C9orf72-initiated disease (S2 context). Packet evidence for pore involvement is associative; kinase identity, sites, and direction are assumptions. Nucleoporin redundancy may buffer single-site mutations; iPSC and mouse models may not reproduce decades-long onset; post-mortem tissue is late-stage; phospho-signals may be transient.

Ranked proposal:
Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 initiates selective nuclear import failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in TDP-43-proteinopathy motor neurons.

In sporadic ALS motor neurons with TDP-43 proteinopathy, sustained stress activates a kinase that phosphorylates Nup98 at FG/GLFG-region sites, weakening the NPC permeability barrier and the rate of facilitated NLS-cargo import. This initiating pore modification reduces nuclear retention and import of TDP-43; cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing, stress-granule-driven sequestration of transport factors, Ran-gradient collapse, and cell death are downstream amplifiers, not the first cause. A3: the directional claim that phosphorylation precedes TDP-43 egress, inverted from S1's co-occurrence. A4: specificity to TDP-43-proteinopathy ALS. Asp/Glu phosphomimetic substitutions are acknowledged as chemically poor phosphate mimics and will anchor no conclusion.

Causal chain (revised). Initiating: kinase activation → Nup98 FG phosphorylation → increased passive permeability and reduced facilitated NLS-import at the pore. Secondary: reduced nuclear TDP-43 retention → cytoplasmic de-mixing (S3) → SG formation and transport-factor sequestration (S4) → Ran-gradient dissipation → cell death. Ran gradient is deliberately decoupled from the initiating lesion: RanGAP/RCC1 localization primarily maintain it, so gradient changes are used as downstream readouts, not bundled into the initiation claim.

(2) Physical displacement: insoluble TDP-43 directly distorts pores (consistent with S1), phosphorylation a bystander. (3) Genetic route: C9orf72 repeat RNA/DPR mechanisms (S2). (4) Reverse causality: late phosphorylation secondary to stress or disassembly.

Discriminating strategy.
• Modification validation first: knock in endogenous tagged Nup98; map phosphorylation sites by MS of purified nuclear-envelope fractions across a stress time course; validate phosphopeptide-specific antibodies against mapped sites, or use chemically inducible kinase recruitment to tagged Nup98 for acute, reversible gain-of-function — this replaces reliance on Asp/Glu phosphomimetics, which remain secondary only.
• Direct attribution: digitonin-permeabilized neurons reconstituted with recombinant phosphorylated versus phospho-null Nup98 (FG-region constructs MS-verified) to measure passive tracer flux and NLS-import kinetics directly attributable to the modification, separating pore effects from import-factor or Ran effects.
• Temporal tests: (i) stress-onset course of Nup98 phospho-occupancy, NLS-reporter import, and TDP-43 localization; (ii) stress pulse–washout: if phosphorylation initiates, the phospho-signal should dissipate before import recovers; import failure persisting after phospho-loss supports a sequestration-first alternative and counters late-bystander phosphorylation.
• Perturbational test with graded predictions: a CRISPR multi-site phospho-null panel (clustered Ala substitutions across the nominated GLFG cluster), interpreted only after MS verification that candidate-site phospho-occupancy is suppressed. Outcome metric: NLS-import decline normalized to SG burden and soluble importin availability, quantified across mild-to-strong stress. Graded prediction: phospho-null neurons show a significantly attenuated early-phase import decline versus wild type at matched SG burden — not full preservation, because S4 establishes SG-independent-of-phosphorylation impairment. Late-phase failure in phospho-null neurons is expected and non-discriminating; only the early phosphorylation-attributable component counts. Interpretation rule: verified occupancy suppression plus an indistinguishable early normalized decline falsifies the hypothesis; failure to suppress occupancy (compensatory kinases/buffering) makes the test uninformative, not falsifying.
• Staged in vivo arm: only after in vitro discrimination, neuron-targeted multi-site Nup98 editing or kinase inhibition in a conditional TDP-43-mislocalization mouse, with import markers, TDP-43 localization, motor behavior, and survival as endpoints; post-mortem ALS tissue immunostained with the validated phospho-Nup98 reagent in neurons lacking cytoplasmic TDP-43 inclusions (early) versus affected neurons (late), as corroboration only.

Falsifying observation. With MS-verified suppression of the targeted Nup98 phospho-cluster (and no compensating phosphorylation at other mapped sites), mild stress produces an early-phase normalized import decline equal to wild type at matched SG burden and soluble importin availability; and in pulse–washout, import failure precedes or outlasts detectable Nup98 phosphorylation. Packet evidence for pore involvement is associative; kinase identity, residues, and direction remain assumptions pending MS confirmation. Asp/Glu mimicry is weak, so gain-of-function relies on inducible kinase recruitment. Buffering is addressed only for the nominated cluster; broader nucleoporin compensation remains possible. iPSC and mouse models may not reproduce decades-long onset; post-mortem tissue is late-stage; phospho-signals are transient.

Ranked proposal:
Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin Nup98 initiates selective nuclear import failure upstream of TDP-43 mislocalization in TDP-43-proteinopathy motor neurons.

Exact NUP62 residues are not established by the packet and must be identified experimentally rather than asserted.

Targeted mass spectrometry should identify increased NUP62 phosphorylation; purified-protein kinase experiments with inactive-kinase controls should test whether p38α can directly generate those modifications. Fix the candidate phosphosite set before subsequent causal comparisons. The hypothesis predicts increased phosphorylation and reduced pore occupancy before import impairment, followed by TDP-43 redistribution and functional decline.

Causal perturbation. Introduce phosphorylation-resistant substitutions at the mapped endogenous NUP62 sites, alongside wild-type revertant controls. Confirm that these substitutions block the candidate modification without changing basal NUP62 abundance, pore occupancy, or import. Complement this substrate-specific intervention with genetic p38α suppression. Protection by phosphorylation-resistant NUP62 despite persistent upstream stress would support a causal pore modification rather than a nonspecific benefit of kinase inhibition. Acute p38α activation in corrected neurons should produce early import impairment only when NUP62 remains phosphorylatable. Because kinase activation affects other substrates, that experiment is persuasive only together with NUP62-site dependence, direct biochemical phosphorylation, and the predicted pore-occupancy change.

The principal alternative is that TDP-43 assemblies or stress granules sequester soluble transport machinery first, while NUP62 phosphorylation follows as a stress response [S3, S4]. p38α-Dependent NUP62 Phosphorylation as an Initiator of Nuclear-Import Failure in TARDBP-Mutant Motor Neurons

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Nup98 phosphorylation by a stress-responsive proline-directed kinase initiates nuclear-pore barrier failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy models of ALS

Hypothesis. In neuronal models of TDP-43 proteinopathy, a setting relevant to ALS and ALS/FTD cases that accumulate cytoplasmic TDP-43, phosphorylation of Nup98, an FG-nucleoporin by unverified prior knowledge, is proposed as the initiating, pore-intrinsic cause of selective nucleocytoplasmic-transport failure. Impaired nuclear import, loss of nuclear TDP-43, growth of cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, and later neuronal dysfunction are the proposed downstream responses. Nucleoporin phosphorylation remains an untested candidate cause.

Supported premises. Nuclear-pore and transport components associate with insoluble TDP-43, and disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in cell systems, with related pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Those findings support a TDP-43-pore connection while leaving the initiating biochemical event and cross-subtype generality unresolved [S1]. In a separate genetic context, expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA is linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons, and transport or repeat-RNA manipulations modify model phenotypes [S2]. This is a C9orf72-specific route and leaves both sporadic ALS and any nucleoporin phosphorylation step unresolved [S2]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, and accompany import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death; phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulates in the assemblies [S3]. That phosphorylation mark is on TDP-43, and the experiments leave open other physiological trajectories [S3]. Cellular stress recruits transport factors into stress granules and impairs transport, and changing stress-granule assembly modifies transport defects and disease-model phenotypes [S4].

Speculative bridges. The kinase, the residues, and the causal order are assumptions. Unverified prior knowledge, held outside this packet and given no citation identifier, is that Nup98 phosphorylation during mitotic or stress signaling can relax nuclear-pore selectivity. The working assumption is that a proline-directed stress-responsive kinase, provisionally CDK5 or ERK1/2, phosphorylates Nup98 FG-repeat or C-terminal residues in post-mitotic neurons expressing pathogenic TDP-43. The proposed sequence is kinase activation, Nup98 phosphorylation, altered NPC barrier function, and only then sequestration of transport factors plus loss of nuclear TDP-43. Nup98 phosphorylation is the initiating pore event. Import failure, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death are downstream responses of the kind reported with cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies [S3]. Scope is limited to TDP-43 proteinopathy models. C9orf72-ALS retains RanGAP mislocalization as a separate entry point [S2].

Alternative explanations. Sequestration of transport receptors and Ran regulators into stress granules [S4], or into stress-granule-independent TDP-43 assemblies [S3], can impair import while nucleoporins themselves remain unmodified. Nucleoporin mislocalization can follow binding to insoluble TDP-43 [S1]. Broad cellular stress can degrade transport without a Nup98 phospho-event. Repeat RNA and RanGAP pathology can account for transport failure in C9orf72 models [S2]. Shared late phenotypes, reduced import and nuclear TDP-43 loss, therefore fail to identify which event came first.

Discriminating preclinical test. Use a neuronal TDP-43 proteinopathy model that develops transport defects, and run a C9orf72 repeat model only as a context comparator. On a time course, measure Nup98 phosphorylation in nuclear-pore fractions by mass spectrometry and phospho-specific blot, Nup98 localization at NPCs, nuclear import of a reporter and of endogenous TDP-43, stress-granule markers, and stress-granule-independent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. The prediction is that Nup98 phosphorylation rises before import falls and before transport factors accumulate in either compartment. A non-phosphorylatable Nup98 that incorporates into NPCs should preserve import when stress granules are induced [S4] and when early cytoplasmic TDP-43 de-mixing is present [S3]. A phosphomimetic Nup98 in otherwise unstressed neurons should impair import without stress granules and before large TDP-43 aggregates. Kinase inhibition should copy the non-phosphorylatable Nup98 result only while those Nup98 sites are intact. If phosphomimetic Nup98 is already installed, blocking stress-granule assembly or TDP-43 de-mixing should leave a residual import defect. The sequestration alternatives predict the complementary pattern: phosphomimetic Nup98 is inert when transport factors remain free, and blocking granules or TDP-43 assemblies restores import regardless of the Nup98 phospho-state.

Falsifying observation. Reject the hypothesis in this model if import failure and nuclear TDP-43 loss occur with a flat Nup98 phosphorylation time course. Reject it if NPC-incorporated non-phosphorylatable Nup98 leaves the onset and size of the transport defect unchanged while stress-granule or TDP-43-assembly interventions fully account for that defect. Reject it if phosphomimetic Nup98 impairs import only when transport factors are sequestered. A phospho-Nup98 rise confined to the C9orf72 comparator, with no rise in the TDP-43 model, rejects the proposed disease context.

Limitations. Sites and kinase identity are assumed, and phosphorylation may be a later mark of pore injury rather than its start. Neuronal cultures omit glia, aging, and circuit context, and partial Nup98 replacement can mask an effect. Phospho-specific reagents can cross-react with phosphorylated TDP-43 or other FG-nucleoporins. Preservation of import by non-phosphorylatable Nup98 would still leave other nucleoporins and the RanGAP axis [S2] open. The experiment tests a mechanism and does not validate a treatment.

Ranked proposal:
Nup98 phosphorylation by a stress-responsive proline-directed kinase initiates nuclear-pore barrier failure in TDP-43 proteinopathy models of ALS

# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
NUP98 Ser606 phosphorylation as an initiating pore lesion in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In motor neurons carrying the ALS-associated TARDBP M337V variant, increased phosphorylation of NUP98 at candidate residue Ser606 reduces NUP98 retention at nuclear pores, initiating impaired nuclear import before detectable cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. Import failure subsequently promotes nuclear TDP-43 depletion, cytoplasmic accumulation, and neuronal dysfunction. Here, “initiating” means initiating the transport defect—not preceding the genetic mutation or explaining every ALS subtype. The variant’s disease association and the selection of NUP98 Ser606 draw on unverified prior knowledge, not the supplied packet.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 can disrupt nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, and pore pathology occurs in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can impair import and accompany nuclear TDP-43 depletion and cell death without conventional stress granules [S3]. Conversely, stress granules can sequester transport factors and disrupt transport [S4]. These observations justify testing a pore–transport–TDP-43 feedback mechanism, but none establishes NUP98 phosphorylation as its starting point. C9orf72 repeat RNA provides a distinct, genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction [S2]; the proposed mechanism should therefore initially be evaluated only in the specified TARDBP context.

Speculative bridges. The hypothesis assumes that mutant TDP-43 changes an unidentified kinase/phosphatase balance, that Ser606 becomes phosphorylated in these neurons, and that this modification weakens pore association rather than merely marking stress. It further assumes that the resulting import defect contributes causally to TDP-43 redistribution and functional decline. These are experimentally separable links within one causal hypothesis, not established findings. No kinase identity or phosphorylation-dependent interaction is supplied by [S1]–[S4].

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Study several independently derived patient motor-neuron lines alongside isogenic TARDBP-corrected controls. First verify the candidate residue against the expressed NUP98 sequence and establish site-localized phosphorylation with targeted mass spectrometry. Across a longitudinal sampling series, quantify Ser606 occupancy relative to total NUP98, pore-associated NUP98, nuclear-import kinetics using a releasable localization reporter, nuclear/cytoplasmic TDP-43, transport-factor sequestration, conventional stress granules, neuronal firing, and survival. Include passive-permeability, energy-status, and general-stress measurements to distinguish import failure from nonspecific cellular deterioration. The predicted sequence is increased phosphorylation, reduced pore-associated NUP98, impaired import, and then TDP-43 redistribution and dysfunction. Temporal precedence alone would not establish causation.

Test necessity by introducing an endogenous phospho-resistant S606A substitution into mutant and corrected lines, with wild-type sequence-reverted controls. Seek orthogonal confirmation through inducible NUP98-directed phosphatase recruitment, using catalytically inactive and untargeted controls and measuring neighboring phosphorylation sites. Both interventions should preserve pore localization and import before substantially changing cytoplasmic assembly burden, followed by improved neuronal function. Verify that neither intervention independently disrupts baseline transport or NUP98 abundance in corrected neurons. For biochemical sufficiency, compare authentic, site-specifically phosphorylated and unphosphorylated NUP98 in a reconstituted pore-association and transport assay without cytoplasmic assemblies. Its feasibility is an assumption; a phosphomimetic substitution alone would provide only provisional evidence.

Alternatives and falsification. Transport-factor sequestration could initiate failure, with NUP98 phosphorylation occurring afterward [S3, S4]; broader stress could independently cause both changes. Compare phosphorylation-directed interventions with independently validated suppression of conventional stress granules and cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies, monitoring intervention effects on phosphorylation and general stress. The proposed ordering predicts an early phosphorylation-dependent defect even when assemblies are suppressed. A decisive falsifying outcome would be verified prevention of Ser606 phosphorylation by two orthogonal interventions, with baseline pore function preserved, yet unchanged timing and magnitude of import failure and neuronal dysfunction. Phosphorylation consistently appearing only after transport failure would also contradict the proposed initiating role.

Limitations. Undetected small assemblies could precede apparent phosphorylation, and phosphatase targeting or amino-acid substitution could have unintended effects. Reconstituted pores cannot establish neuronal sufficiency, and cultured motor neurons may omit aging and non-neuronal influences. Positive findings would support a bounded mechanism in this TARDBP context, not a validated treatment or universal ALS cause.

Ranked proposal:
NUP98 Ser606 phosphorylation as an initiating pore lesion in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
FG-region NUP98 phosphorylation by reactivated CDK1 initiates Ran-gradient failure after nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In motor neurons carrying ALS-associated TARDBP M337V, nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction promotes CDK1 phosphorylation of NUP98 inside its FG/GLFG cohesive region. That modification initiates the transport lesion: it weakens FG cohesion, raises size-selective passive permeability, and collapses the Ran/NTF2 gradient before persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies appear. Import failure then deepens nuclear TDP-43 loss, permits cytoplasmic demixing, and drives neuronal dysfunction. “Initiating” means the start of the transport defect in this TARDBP context. The M337V association, CDK1 identity, and FG-domain biology are unverified prior knowledge. C9orf72 repeat RNA is a separate route to RanGAP mislocalization and import failure [S2] and is a boundary contrast, not support for this initiator.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, and pore pathology occurs in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form without conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, impair import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, and accompany cell death; phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulates in those assemblies [S3]. Cellular stress can also sequester transport factors in stress granules and impair transport [S4]. No supplied source identifies a nucleoporin phosphorylation event or its order relative to TDP-43 dysfunction.

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge holds that NUP98’s N-terminal FG/GLFG repeats cohere to set passive permeability, that its C-terminal domain anchors it at the pore, and that mitotic CDK1 phosphorylation of NUP98 promotes NPC disassembly. The hypothesis assumes that partial FG-restricted phosphorylation in postmitotic neurons can increase permeability and disturb the Ran gradient without full NPC disassembly. It assumes nuclear mutant TDP-43 alters splicing of a CDK1 regulator or an opposing phosphatase so CDK1 occupancy on NUP98 rises. It assumes the import defect is sufficient for later TDP-43 redistribution. Any claim that phosphorylated TDP-43 causes demixing is untested; [S3] only places phosphorylated TDP-43 inside assemblies. No kinase, residue, or phosphorylation-dependent contact is given by [S1]–[S4].

Alternatives. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 demixing [S3] or stress-granule sequestration of transport factors [S4] may impair transport first, with NUP98 phosphorylation appearing afterward. Generic proteostatic or metabolic stress may shift phosphorylation and transport together. Phosphorylation confined to the NUP98 anchor domain, or of another nucleoporin, may account for the pore phenotype. Repeat-RNA mechanisms [S2] stay outside this TARDBP test. GSK3β or JNK marking is a competing stress-kinase explanation.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Study independently derived TARDBP M337V iPSC motor neurons and isogenic corrected controls, without an exogenous TDP-43 inducer. Live-cell imaging and bulk biochemistry share a pre-registered maturation clock. Define t0 from live imaging as the first window in which mutant import of a releasable NLS reporter diverges from corrected cells by a pre-set effect size. At matched earlier and later windows, measure a nuclear TDP-43 splicing target that encodes a CDK1 regulator or opposing phosphatase; CDK1–NUP98 occupancy versus GSK3β and JNK occupancy; NPC immunoprecipitate phosphoproteomics; pore-associated NUP98; size-resolved passive permeability; the Ran gradient; transport-factor localization; conventional stress granules; cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies; firing and survival; and energy status plus general-stress markers.

Site acceptance is pre-registered and precedes allele engineering. A residue must be detected on endogenous NUP98, enriched in mutant neurons at or before t0, map in the FG/GLFG region rather than solely in the anchoring domain, and match a CDK consensus. If no residue qualifies, engineering stops and the FG–CDK1 hypothesis fails in this model. If one or more qualify, introduce endogenous phospho-resistant substitutions and a separate CDK1 loss-of-function allele, each with sequence-reverted and kinase-intact controls. Add acute NUP98-directed phosphatase recruitment with catalytically inactive and untargeted controls. In corrected neurons these reagents must preserve NUP98 abundance, baseline permeability, and import. Expression of nuclear-retained wild-type TDP-43 in mutant neurons, versus a cytoplasmic-restricted control, tests whether phosphorylation tracks nuclear TDP-43 function. Separate suppression of cytoplasmic TDP-43 demixing and of conventional stress-granule assembly asks whether the early permeability and Ran defects remain when those downstream events are blocked. Sufficiency uses site-specifically phosphorylated versus unmodified NUP98 in a reconstituted FG-cohesion and permeability assay; only a biochemically validated phosphomimetic is then introduced into unstressed corrected neurons, with confirmation of normal pore incorporation.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is falsified if no qualifying FG-region phosphorylation precedes t0, or if two orthogonal interventions that prevent that phosphorylation and preserve baseline pore function leave the timing and magnitude of import failure, Ran-gradient loss, and neuronal dysfunction unchanged. A splicing defect that appears only after phosphorylation, or phosphorylation that falls when general-stress markers fall while the nuclear TDP-43 splicing defect persists, also contradicts the proposed order. A phosphomimetic that fails the reconstituted permeability test is inconclusive.

Limitations. Undetected small assemblies, redundant kinases, and additional phosphosites can hide single-site effects. Phosphatase recruitment and amino-acid substitution can act off-target. NUP98 also functions in mRNA export and chromatin contacts. Reconstituted assays omit neuronal context, and cultured motor neurons omit aging and non-cell-autonomous influences. A positive result would support a bounded TARDBP mechanism, not a validated treatment or a cause shared by every ALS subtype.

Ranked proposal:
FG-region NUP98 phosphorylation by reactivated CDK1 initiates Ran-gradient failure after nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML

CORE HYPOTHESIS. Teriflunomide (the active molecule corresponding to the leflunomide class; original indication: relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, with leflunomide historically approved for rheumatoid/psoriatic arthritis - approval facts are unverified prior knowledge to be confirmed against the regulatory label) reaches clinically achievable free concentrations that inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) in AML blasts. Blocking DHODH-mediated conversion of dihydroorotate to orotate (textbook biochemistry, outside-packet general knowledge) depletes de novo pyrimidine synthesis, releases the myeloid differentiation block, and drives terminal maturation with cell-cycle exit. The hypothesis is only claimed for differentiation-blocked AML contexts where the dominant residual pathology is an immature, lineage-blocked blast population; it is not a stem-cell-eradication claim and teriflunomide is not an established AML regimen.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (from the packet).
- P1 (S4, core): DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and altered disease-related endpoints in experimental AML, linking pyrimidine metabolism to the differentiative state. S4 explicitly does not establish that every approved drug acting on this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity; closing exactly that gap is the purpose of this hypothesis.
- P2 (S2, context): chemotherapy-persistent AML cells were not consistently LSC-enriched but depended on oxidative metabolism, showing that residual disease contains metabolically definable, targetable states distinct from bulk untreated biology.
- P3 (S1, framing): quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells were BCL-2-dependent and OXPHOS-linked, demonstrating that AML populations can carry selective metabolic liabilities (e.g., venetoclax-class sensitivity). This motivates selectivity reasoning only; it does not predict DHODH effects on LSCs.
- P4 (S3, comparator): venetoclax-azacitidine showed patient-associated TCA-cycle/OXPHOS changes in leukemia stem-enriched cells, providing an established metabolic-mechanism comparator and a biomarker template. No packet source supports teriflunomide efficacy in AML; that gap is what the hypothesis proposes to test.

EXPLICITLY SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (assumptions, not evidence).
- B1: clinically achievable free teriflunomide exceeds the DHODH inhibitory threshold in blasts. Teriflunomide is reportedly highly protein-bound with a long half-life (unverified prior knowledge); B1 is the central quantitative assumption and may fail.
- B2: blasts depend on de novo pyrimidine synthesis despite plasma uridine salvage, and normal CD34+ cells depend less, yielding a therapeutic window. Indirectly consistent with S4, but unproven for this drug and compartment.
- B3: because DHODH donates electrons into the CoQ/respiratory chain, inhibition might additionally perturb respiration in the OXPHOS-dependent residual cells of S2. Conjecture, treated only as a secondary endpoint.

1) Engagement: LC-MS quantification of the dihydroorotate:orotate ratio and UTP/CTP pools in primary blast cultures from a genomically diverse panel (NPM1-mutant, FLT3-ITD, TP53-mutant, MLL-rearranged) at free-fraction-matched teriflunomide concentrations derived from label pharmacokinetics.

6) Only after single-agent validation, exploratory testing of teriflunomide added to an HMA or venetoclax in residual-disease protocols, using S3 as the established comparator rather than as the proposal itself.

At free concentrations matching clinically achievable exposure: (a) no DHODH engagement in blasts; or (b) engagement without differentiation (only cytostasis/apoptosis); or (c) differentiation effects that are neither rescued by pyrimidines nor modified by DHODH genetic state; or (d) comparable killing of normal CD34+ colonies. Multi-week half-life implies slow pharmacodynamics and delayed response assessment (unverified label detail); known class risks include immunosuppression, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity, all requiring label confirmation; murine xenografts poorly model human pyrimidine salvage; I cannot verify from the packet whether teriflunomide or leflunomide has been tested in AML, so if comparable data exist the novelty claim must be re-scoped; investigational DHODH inhibitors in AML development are not approved drugs and do not satisfy, nor pre-empt, the repurposing question posed here.

Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for differentiation-blocked AML

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

Hypothesis: In cytarabine-residual AML with an oxidative metabolic phenotype, persistent differentiation blockade, and low functional uridine-salvage capacity, clinically achievable unbound teriflunomide exposure will inhibit DHODH, deplete pyrimidine pools, and induce durable myeloid differentiation. This should reduce leukemia-propagating capacity while relatively sparing normal hematopoietic progenitors. Low salvage capacity, rather than oxidative metabolism alone, is the proposed determinant of sensitivity.

Supported premises: DHODH inhibition promoted differentiation and affected disease-related endpoints in experimental AML systems [S4]. Cytarabine-resistant AML cells displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties but were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells [S2]. These findings justify investigating a differentiation-directed metabolic intervention in residual disease, but neither establishes teriflunomide efficacy. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem-cell population described in [S1] must therefore be analyzed separately rather than equated with all residual AML. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established energy-metabolism comparator, not a new repurposing proposal [S3].

Drug premise and speculative bridges: Teriflunomide’s approval for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and its DHODH-inhibitory activity are unverified prior knowledge here; the packet does not verify either claim. Another unverified biochemical premise is that extracellular uridine salvage can replenish pyrimidines despite DHODH inhibition. Regulatory status, target pharmacology, and human unbound exposure require independent confirmation before experimentation. The central speculative bridge is that a subset of residual AML cannot salvage enough uridine under marrow conditions to compensate for DHODH inhibition. Further assumptions are that achievable drug exposure crosses this metabolic threshold, nucleotide depletion produces differentiation rather than only arrest or death, and normal progenitors retain sufficient compensatory capacity. Oxidative metabolism is not assumed to prove DHODH dependence.

Discriminating preclinical strategy: Study paired pretreatment and cytarabine-residual patient-derived AML samples, supplemented by residual-disease xenografts. Before drug treatment, measure respiration and quantify functional salvage using labeled uridine incorporation into pyrimidine nucleotides under physiologically justified uridine conditions. Include both low- and high-salvage AML, and normal donor CD34-positive progenitors. Use stromal coculture and protein-containing media, directly measure unbound drug, and restrict efficacy conclusions to independently verified human-compatible exposures. Establish temporal ordering by measuring DHODH-pathway metabolites and nucleotide pools before apoptosis, respiratory collapse, or maturation. Score differentiation using blinded morphology and mature-myeloid immunophenotypes in cells confirmed to retain the leukemia genotype; this guards against mistaking surviving normal cells or selective blast killing for malignant-cell differentiation.

Mechanistic discrimination: Compare teriflunomide with vehicle, an independently characterized DHODH inhibitor, and established venetoclax–azacitidine [S3]. DHODH suppression should phenocopy the differentiation response. Uridine supplementation should reverse differentiation when isotope tracing confirms restoration of pyrimidine pools, without reducing drug exposure. These interventions distinguish on-pathway nucleotide limitation from unrelated drug toxicity. Measure viable malignant-cell output, apoptosis, and colony formation separately. In randomized xenografts, determine free plasma and marrow exposure, then test leukemia-propagating capacity by limiting-dilution secondary transplantation after drug washout. Assess normal progenitor colony formation and normal hematopoietic engraftment in parallel; reduced AML viability alone does not demonstrate selectivity or stem-cell depletion.

Alternatives, falsification, and limitations: Apparent maturation could reflect differential survival of pre-existing mature cells, generic cytostasis, or off-target toxicity. Marrow-derived uridine could abolish a response seen in simplified culture. The central falsifying observation would be confirmed DHODH engagement and sustained pyrimidine depletion in predicted low-salvage residual AML without genuine differentiation or reduced leukemia-propagating capacity. Persistence of the response after verified pyrimidine-pool rescue would instead contradict the proposed causal mechanism. Failure to engage DHODH at human-compatible exposure would reject translational feasibility. Heterogeneous salvage capacity, microenvironmental rescue, uncertain marrow pharmacokinetics, and normal-cell toxicity remain major limitations. The packet supports a pathway rationale, not this drug’s therapeutic window, clinical benefit, or novelty.

Ranked proposal:
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, relieves differentiation blockade in human AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at exposures separable from venetoclax–azacitidine oxidative-phosphorylation suppression.

Biological context and hypothesis. The claim covers primary human AML only when viable blasts have a fraction positive for any of CD11b, CD14, or CD15 below 20% and morphologic myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and monocytes together below 10%. In that gated population, teriflunomide will induce cell-intrinsic myeloid maturation by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) at free concentrations at or below the unbound plasma maximum of its approved multiple-sclerosis dose, with normal CD34-positive colony formation retained at or above 70% of vehicle. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in those models, tying that result to myeloid maturation. [S4] leaves open whether an approved drug reproduces that result at suitable exposure and selectivity. [S1] reports that leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens often had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S3] connects venetoclax–azacitidine, an established regimen and mechanistic comparator, to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes in leukemia stem cells. Repeating that combination is not the proposed discovery. [S2] reports that cytarabine-residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells and showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, so residual disease and the ROS-low population are distinct contexts.

Speculative bridges, labeled as such. Unverified prior knowledge requiring source checking: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis and is described as a DHODH inhibitor; brequinar is the experimental DHODH inhibitor associated with the differentiation result summarized by [S4]; suppression is read as dihydroorotate accumulation and uridine-triphosphate depletion; and exogenous uridine bypasses a DHODH block. Bridge one: multiple-sclerosis-compatible free exposure inhibits DHODH in gated blasts enough to recapitulate [S4]. Bridge two, which [S4] alone does not entail: when dihydroorotate and uridine-triphosphate changes match brequinar, maturation scales with the depth of pyrimidine-pool depletion. Bridge three: maturation is dissociable from loss of ROS-low, BCL-2-high leukemia stem cells [S1] and from the cytarabine-residual oxidative state [S2]. Hypothesis: At clinically attainable unbound exposure, atovaquone will inhibit respiratory-complex-III-supported DHODH activity sufficiently to induce differentiation and reduce leukemia propagation in cytarabine-residual AML with persistent oxidative metabolism and limited pyrimidine salvage. The ROS-low, BCL-2-associated population described in [S1] should be assessed separately rather than used as a synonym for residual disease. Venetoclax–azacitidine provides an established metabolic comparator, not the proposed repurposing discovery [S3].

A second, explicitly uncertain bridge is that salvage-limited residual AML will differentiate under this restriction while normal hematopoietic progenitors retain sufficient functional capacity. Neither bridge follows automatically from an oxidative phenotype.

Separate biochemical assays of complex III and DHODH should test whether the drug acts through respiration rather than directly inhibiting DHODH.

Compare vehicle, a reference DHODH inhibitor, and venetoclax–azacitidine as the established comparator [S3]. The decisive epistasis experiments are uridine supplementation and expression of a validated respiratory-chain-independent DHODH construct. Both should restore pyrimidine pools and prevent atovaquone-induced maturation and propagation loss without restoring respiratory inhibition. Rescue performance must first be validated against the reference DHODH inhibitor. # AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Title: Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML that still shows a differentiation block, relies on de novo pyrimidine synthesis, and retains oxidative metabolism, atovaquone at a verified unbound exposure will inhibit respiratory complex III, shrink the oxidized ubiquinone pool, and thereby restrict DHODH long enough to induce genotype-confirmed myeloid maturation and lower leukemia propagation. The intended mediator is pyrimidine depletion with ATP still intact. The original indication is treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis pneumonia, and atovaquone plus proguanil for malaria; those label facts, reported protein binding above 99.9%, and any mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge and must be confirmed before exposure claims are made.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells in the studied models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. Separately, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a distinct population and a selectivity benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is only the established metabolic comparator [S3]. Nothing in [S2] or [S4] shows that residual cells are DHODH-dependent or salvage-limited; that gap is a go/no-go, not an assumption.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1: ubiquinone redox restriction will suppress DHODH before nonspecific energetic failure at unbound levels that do not exceed label-verified unbound Cmax. Bridge 2: residual cells that pass the gates below will mature, whereas normal progenitors in a matched cycling state will keep colony-forming capacity. Bridge 3: a functional respiratory chain can support DHODH, so an oxidative phenotype is a complex III entry point, while pyrimidine dependence is set by de novo-versus-salvage flux. Human DHODH use of oxidized ubiquinone, uridine bypass of de novo synthesis, and the properties of Saccharomyces cerevisiae URA1 (cytosolic, fumarate-linked, respiratory-chain-independent type 1 DHODH) are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of leflunomide (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide itself approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor, not the repurposing claim.

Preclinical strategy. Lock gates on the same primary specimens before any atovaquone attribution. Eligibility requires a cytarabine pulse and washout, residual oxygen consumption with an etomoxir-sensitive fraction at least 1.5-fold matched pretreatment blasts, proliferation recorded as a covariate, baseline CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed cells with blast morphology, and salvage limitation defined by tracer partitioning (at least half of UTP from the de novo route) or by uridine reversing at least 70% of the reference inhibitor’s nucleotide and maturation effects. Labeled-uridine incorporation is only a cycling covariate. ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and pretreatment bulk blasts are separate arms. The go/no-go requires teriflunomide, in protein-containing medium, to raise dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold and CD11b by at least 15 percentage points while ATP stays within 20% of vehicle, with uridine reversing both. Failure aborts the atovaquone test in that context. Isolated-enzyme assays must show atovaquone inhibits complex III and spares DHODH, and teriflunomide the reverse. Measure free atovaquone; the translational claim fails if the free EC50 for a twofold dihydroorotate:orotate shift exceeds label-verified unbound Cmax. A time gate must show ubiquinone reduction and pyrimidine-flux change while ATP loss is still under 20% and before maturation. Coincident ATP collapse makes the run uninterpretable and stops it. In an engineered line, induce URA1 only after the residual state is established and prove that pyrimidine restoration leaves complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact. Uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide; if either rescue fails against teriflunomide, stop. Later endpoints are morphology plus the marker panel, absolute viable counts, apoptosis, and post-washout clonogenicity. Selectivity fails if normal CD34-positive colony inhibition at the free EC50 is within threefold of AML. Only after these gates, cytarabine-primed xenografts test marrow free drug, differentiation, limiting-dilution initiating-cell frequency (prespecified threefold reduction), and normal hematopoietic recovery. A documented search must separate this residual-state, salvage-gated, ubiquinone-timed claim from any published atovaquone or leflunomide AML work; this packet does not establish novelty.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation can reflect preferential loss of immature cells, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other atovaquone targets, or ATP collapse. The relationship is falsified, even if atovaquone remains cytotoxic, if validated uridine and URA1 rescues restore pyrimidine pools and leave complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact yet differentiation and at least a threefold clonogenic loss persist, while the same rescues reverse teriflunomide.

Limitations. Protein binding may leave no unbound window; proliferating normal progenitors may be equally sensitive; differentiation need not durably clear leukemia; [S2] models may differ from clinical marrow; [S4] does not transfer across genotypes; murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Exposure, construct biochemistry, and prior AML studies require external verification.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss
