# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis — FG-region NUP98 phosphorylation by a TDP-43-dysregulated WEE1–CDC25C/CDK1 axis initiates Ran-gradient collapse before cytoplasmic TDP-43 demixing in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

In isogenic human iPSC-derived motor neurons carrying TARDBP M337V, nuclear mutant-TDP-43 dysfunction—assayed before any cytoplasmic assembly—mis-splices the WEE1 and CDC25C transcripts, tilting the CDK1 activation axis. Raised CDK1 activity then phosphorylates NUP98 within its N-terminal FG/GLFG repeat region; that lesion weakens FG cohesion, raises size-selective passive permeability, and collapses the Ran/NTF2-L1 gradient, initiating import failure. Import failure then deepens nuclear TDP-43 depletion, fosters cytoplasmic demixing, and drives dysfunction and death. "Initiating" denotes the start of the transport lesion in this TARDBP context, not a universal ALS cause; the C9orf72 repeat-RNA route to RanGAP mislocalization and import failure [S2] is a boundary contrast, not support.

Supported premises. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, with pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can form independently of conventional stress granules, mislocalize transport-associated proteins, impair import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, and accompany cell death, with phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulating in these assemblies [S3]. Cellular stress can alternatively sequester transport factors into stress granules and impair transport [S4]. No supplied source identifies a nucleoporin phosphorylation event, kinase, residue, or ordering.

Speculative bridges. Unverified prior knowledge holds that NUP98 FG/GLFG repeats cohere to set passive permeability, that a C-terminal region anchors it at the pore, and that mitotic CDK1 phosphorylation of NUP98 promotes NPC disassembly. Assumed, not evidenced from the packet: (a) partial FG-restricted phosphorylation in postmitotic neurons raises permeability without full disassembly; (b) WEE1 and CDC25C are TDP-43 splicing substrates whose correctly spliced isoforms restrain CDK1, so nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction raises CDK1 occupancy on NUP98; (c) early import failure suffices to drive later TDP-43 redistribution. Whether phosphorylated TDP-43 promotes demixing is untested; [S3] only places it inside assemblies.

Discriminating preclinical strategy. Use several independently derived M337V iPSC motor-neuron lines and isogenic corrected controls, without exogenous TDP-43 inducer, under one pre-registered maturation clock. Stage 1 grounds the site empirically: enrich native NPCs, run comparative phosphoproteomics across the isogenic pair over a dense sampling grid, and quantify candidate sites by targeted LC-MS/MS (PRM/SRM) against synthetic phospho-peptide standards to set a detection floor. t0 is the first grid window in which mutant import of a releasable NLS reporter diverges from corrected cells by a pre-set effect size; strict precedence requires a qualifying site at least one interval before t0. Site acceptance is pre-registered: detected on endogenous NUP98, mutant-enriched before t0, located inside the FG/GLFG region rather than the anchor domain, and matching a CDK consensus; if no residue qualifies, engineering stops and the hypothesis fails. The upstream bridge carries its own order requirement and occlusion test: the WEE1/CDC25C splicing lesion must precede phosphorylation, and inducible expression of a siRNA-resistant, correctly spliced WEE1 allele before t0 must normalize phosphorylation. Direct kinase logic is verified by purified CDK1 phosphorylating the native NUP98 fragment at that site and by epistasis between analog-sensitive CDK1 inhibition and the site substitution, with no additive rescue expected if phosphorylation is the relevant CDK1 output. Necessity arms introduce endogenous phospho-resistant Ala substitutions and, orthogonally, inducible NUP98-directed phosphatase recruitment (catalytically inactive and untargeted controls), each leaving NUP98 abundance, permeability, and import unchanged in corrected neurons. Sufficiency compares authentic, site-specifically phosphorylated and unmodified NUP98 in a reconstituted FG-cohesion/permeability assay, and in-cell an analog-sensitive CDK1 allele or NUP98-targeted kinase-recruitment module installs and reverses the native modification on demand; the phosphomimetic is retained only as a lower-bound approximation. Concurrent readouts: nuclear-retained wild-type TDP-43 versus a cytoplasmic-restricted control in mutant neurons; independent suppression of cytoplasmic demixing [S3] and of conventional stress-granule assembly [S4]; Ran/NTF2-L1 flux alongside size-resolved passive permeability to separate FG-leakage from active-transport failure; CDK1 versus GSK3β/JNK pore occupancy; and energy plus general-stress markers.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis fails if: (1) no qualifying FG-region phosphorylation precedes t0 at the validated detection floor; (2) two orthogonal interventions that prevent that phosphorylation while preserving baseline pore function leave the timing and magnitude of import failure, Ran-gradient loss, and neuronal dysfunction unchanged; (3) timed analog-sensitive CDK1 inhibition immediately before t0 fails to abolish the transport lesion; (4) the WEE1/CDC25C splicing lesion appears only after phosphorylation; or (5) nuclear-retained TDP-43 rescue fails to normalize CDK1 occupancy and phosphorylation even when demixing is suppressed. A phosphomimetic that fails the reconstituted assay is inconclusive, not falsifying.

Alternative explanations. Cytoplasmic demixing-first [S3] or stress-granule sequestration-first [S4] ordering; generic proteostatic or metabolic stress coupling phosphorylation and transport together; phosphorylation of the anchor domain or another nucleoporin; and a GSK3β- or JNK-driven stress-kinase account. The C9orf72 route [S2] stays outside this test.

Limitations. Low-stoichiometry sites, redundant kinases, and multiple phosphosites can mask single-site effects; genome editing and phosphatase recruitment can act off-target; NUP98 also mediates mRNA export and chromatin contacts; reconstituted assays and cultured motor neurons omit aging and non-cell-autonomous context. A positive result supports a bounded, TARDBP-specific initiating mechanism, not a validated treatment or universal cause.

Ranked proposal:
FG-region NUP98 phosphorylation by a TDP-43-dysregulated WEE1–CDC25C/CDK1 axis initiates Ran-gradient collapse before cytoplasmic TDP-43 demixing in TARDBP-mutant motor neurons

Hypothesis. In TARDBP M337V motor neurons, nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction first changes WEE1 splicing so inhibitory control of CDK1 falls. Reactivated CDK1 then phosphorylates NUP98 in its FG/GLFG region. That modification initiates the transport lesion in this TARDBP context: FG cohesion weakens, size-selective passive permeability rises, and Ran/NTF2 flux collapses before persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies. Phosphorylated TDP-43 inside assemblies [S3] is not evidence that it causes demixing. No kinase, residue, or contact is given by [S1]–[S4].

A pilot cohort fixes the calendar day when NLS-reporter import is expected to diverge. The test cohort is sampled every 12 hours from 72 hours before that day through 48 hours after. t0 is the first test-cohort window where mutant import diverges by a pre-set effect size. Qualifying phosphorylation must appear in an earlier bin, above a pre-registered stoichiometry, by PRM/SRM against heavy synthetic phospho-peptide standards. A site is absent only when unmodified peptide and NPC input meet a pre-registered floor and the phospho-peptide is below the limit of detection; low-input samples are inconclusive. The same bins pair import with phospho-site proximity ligation so order is cell-wise, not only bulk.

The WEE1 lesion, scored as loss of the inhibitory isoform plus lower CDK1 Tyr15 phosphorylation, must precede NUP98 phosphorylation. Rescue expresses that inhibitory WEE1 cDNA versus kinase-dead WEE1. The bridge is accepted only if Tyr15 phosphorylation returns and later FG phosphorylation is occluded. Acute pre-t0 CDK1 inhibition, after the splice window and with baseline pore function preserved, must prevent the t0 lesion. Nuclear-retained wild-type TDP-43, versus a cytoplasmic-restricted control, tests whether the splice lesion tracks nuclear TDP-43 function.

The residue must be on endogenous NUP98, enriched strictly before t0, mapped to the FG/GLFG region, and phosphorylated at that exact site by purified CDK1–cyclin B, blocked by a CDK1 inhibitor. Consensus or occupancy alone does not qualify. Phospho-resistant endogenous alleles are then combined with acute CDK1 inhibition: inhibition must remove the site, and transport benefit must disappear when the site cannot be phosphorylated. Residual benefit on the resistant allele means an indirect effect. GSK3β and JNK occupancy are measured in parallel. Suppression of cytoplasmic demixing and of stress-granule assembly tests whether early permeability and Ran defects remain.

Each bin reports passive permeability with size-resolved inert probes and Ran/NTF2 flux as NTF2 nuclear accumulation rate plus Ran-gradient slope. The initiator predicts higher leakage and lower flux before assemblies or stress granules.

In-cell sufficiency installs the native phosphate briefly in unstressed corrected neurons by chemically induced recruitment of an active CDK1 domain to endogenous NUP98, or by analog-sensitive CDK1 with a bulky ATP analog, with kinase-dead and untargeted controls. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. ## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. - These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
## Premature CDK1 phosphorylation of the NUP98 FG/GLFG cohesive region initiates Ran-gradient collapse after nuclear TDP-43 splicing dysfunction in TARDBP M337V motor neurons

**Hypothesis and causal chain.** In iPSC motor neurons carrying ALS-linked TARDBP M337V, early nuclear TDP-43 dysfunction—before detectable cytoplasmic assemblies—misregulates splicing of CDK-axis regulators, permitting partial premature CDK1 activity in postmitotic neurons. CDK1 phosphorylates NUP98 within its FG/GLFG cohesive region; this modification is the **initiating transport lesion**: it locally weakens FG cohesion, increases size-selective passive permeability, and collapses the Ran/NTF2 gradient. Import failure then deepens nuclear TDP-43 depletion, enables cytoplasmic demixing, and drives neuronal dysfunction as a **downstream feed-forward response**, later joined by transport-factor sequestration. "Initiating" means the phosphorylation starts the transport defect in this TARDBP context; it neither precedes the mutation nor generalizes to sporadic ALS, and C9orf72 repeat RNA provides a separate, genetic-context-specific route to RanGAP mislocalization and import failure [S2].

**Supported premises.** Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupts nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport, with pore pathology in ALS tissue [S1]. Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies can impair import, deplete nuclear TDP-43, and accompany cell death independently of conventional stress granules; phosphorylated TDP-43 appears in those assemblies, but this is not nucleoporin phosphorylation [S3]. Stress granules can also sequester transport factors and disrupt transport [S4]. No supplied source identifies a nucleoporin phosphorylation event, its kinase, site, or ordering relative to TDP-43 dysfunction.

**Speculative bridges (assumptions, not findings).** Unverified prior knowledge: NUP98's N-terminal FG/GLFG repeats cohere to set passive permeability while its C-terminal region anchors it at the pore, and mitotic CDK1 phosphorylation of NUP98 promotes NPC disassembly. Assumption 1: partial FG-restricted phosphorylation in postmitotic neurons raises permeability without full pore disassembly. Assumption 2: nuclear mutant TDP-43 mis-splices named candidate transcripts with CDK-axis function—WEE1, CDC25A/C, or a splice-regulated CDK transcript—creating a splicing lesion that temporally precedes NUP98 phosphorylation. Assumption 3: the import defect is sufficient to drive TDP-43 redistribution.

**Alternative explanations.** Cytoplasmic demixing [S3] or stress-granule sequestration [S4] may impair transport first, with NUP98 phosphorylation afterward; generic proteostatic or metabolic stress may raise phosphorylation nonspecifically; a stress kinase (GSK3β or JNK) rather than CDK1 may commit the modification; phosphorylation may occur outside the FG region. These are tested, not assumed away.

**Discriminating preclinical strategy.** Study several independently derived TARDBP M337V iPSC motor-neuron lines and isogenic corrected controls, without exogenous TDP-43 inducer, under a pre-registered maturation clock with high-frequency interleaved live/endpoint sampling, so temporal order is not an artifact of coarse windows and single-cell imaging can order import defects within individual cells. Single-cell live import imaging (releasable NLS reporter) defines t0 prospectively as the first window of pre-registered divergence. At matched pre-t0 and post-t0 windows, measure: candidate splicing lesions, WEE1/CDC25 protein, and CDK1 axis activity (including inhibitory CDK1 phosphorylation); size-resolved passive permeability alongside Ran/NTF2 flux to separate increased leakage from impaired active transport; the Ran gradient; NPC phosphoproteomics with targeted PRM/SRM against synthetic phospho-peptide standards at a pre-registered detection threshold, so low-stoichiometry FG-region sites are not missed; pore-associated NUP98; stress granules; cytoplasmic assemblies; general-stress markers; firing and survival.

**Site gate, before any allele engineering.** A candidate site must be detected on endogenous NUP98, enriched in mutant neurons at or before t0 (strictly before), map to the FG/GLFG region rather than solely the anchor, and be recapitulated in vitro on the identical site by purified recombinant CDK1—consensus matching, kinase occupancy, and CDK1 loss-of-function alone do not establish direct CDK1 phosphorylation. CDK1 versus GSK3β/JNK occupancy is measured to weigh kinase alternatives. The upstream bridge is accepted only if (i) a candidate splicing lesion precedes phosphorylation and (ii) a timed pre-t0 analog-sensitive CDK1-inhibition or WEE1-rescue window abolishes the t0 transport lesion while the splicing lesion persists (occlusion test).

If a site qualifies: introduce endogenous phospho-resistant substitution (sequence-reverted, kinase-intact controls) combined with acute CDK1 perturbation as epistasis, plus acute NUP98-directed phosphatase recruitment (catalytic-dead, untargeted controls) that must preserve corrected-neuron NUP98 abundance, permeability, and import. Sufficiency: authentic site-specifically phosphorylated versus unmodified NUP98 in reconstituted FG-cohesion/permeability assays; then in-cell sufficiency via NUP98-targeted kinase recruitment or an analog-sensitive CDK1 allele that installs and reverses the native modification on demand; a phosphomimetic is retained only as a lower-bound approximation after in vitro validation and confirmed pore incorporation. TDP-43 specificity: express nuclear-retained WT TDP-43 in mutant neurons versus a cytoplasmic-restricted control; phosphorylation normalization must track nuclear rescue, not residual stress signatures. Independently validated suppression of cytoplasmic demixing and conventional stress granules should leave early permeability and Ran defects intact if the hypothesis is correct.

**Falsifying observation.** Falsified if no qualifying CDK1-recapitulated FG-region phosphorylation precedes t0, or if two orthogonal interventions that prevent phosphorylation and preserve baseline pore function leave the timing and magnitude of import failure, Ran-gradient collapse, and dysfunction unchanged. Also falsifying: phosphorylation tracking general-stress markers rather than nuclear TDP-43 rescue, or pre-t0 timed CDK1 inhibition failing to abolish the t0 lesion while the splicing lesion persists. A phosphomimetic failing the reconstituted test is inconclusive, not falsifying.

**Limitations.** Redundant kinases and additional sites can mask single-site effects; targeting and substitution can act off-target; NUP98 also functions in mRNA export and chromatin contact; reconstituted and cultured systems omit aging and non-cell-autonomous contributions. A positive result supports a bounded TARDBP mechanism, not a validated treatment or a cause shared by every ALS subtype.

Ranked proposal:
Premature CDK1 phosphorylation of the NUP98 FG/GLFG cohesive region initiates Ran-gradient collapse after nuclear TDP-43 splicing dysfunction in TARDBP M337V motor neurons

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Title: Teriflunomide repurposing as a DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism AML

Hypothesis. In AML with an oxidative-metabolism phenotype — specifically cytarabine-resistant residual disease and quiescent ROS-low stem-cell-enriched fractions — teriflunomide, an oral drug approved for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (original indication; exact regulatory details require verification), will achieve unbound concentrations that inhibit DHODH, the respiratory-chain-coupled enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. Prediction: pyrimidine-dependent proliferation arrest plus myeloid differentiation, with preferential depletion of these metabolically dependent populations. On-mechanism activity is claimed only if effects are reproduced by genetic DHODH loss and reversed by uridine or orotic-acid repletion that restores pyrimidine pools.

Supported premises (evidence packet).
- [S1] Functionally defined leukemia stem cells were enriched for ROS-low quiescent cells with elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent LSCs. This establishes a quiescent, OxPhos-linked dependency; it does not show that any mitochondrial-pathway drug has a therapeutic window.
- [S2] Cells remaining after cytarabine were not LSC-enriched but showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked features, and altering that state changed treatment response. This defines the resistant-disease context and explicitly cautions that residual cells are not the same population as in [S1].
- [S4] DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML, linking metabolism to reversal of the differentiation blockade rather than nonspecific killing.
- [S3] Reported disruption of LSC energy metabolism by venetoclax-azacitidine provides an established mechanistic comparator showing that metabolism-directed AML therapy can translate to patients; it is cited only as a benchmark, not part of the repurposing claim.

Speculative bridges (explicitly labeled).
1. Drug-to-enzyme bridge: that teriflunomide's active metabolite inhibits DHODH is standard pharmacology recalled from memory — unverified prior knowledge needing label and literature confirmation.
2. Exposure bridge: whether unbound, protein-binding-adjusted teriflunomide levels inhibit DHODH in AML blasts is unknown and is the central quantitative risk.
3. Biochemical bridge: DHODH donates electrons to the respiratory chain (recalled biochemistry, unverified); OxPhos-dependent residual cells [S2] might therefore be preferentially dependent, but DHODH could equally act as pyrimidine restriction independent of respiratory phenotype.
4. Endpoint bridge: [S4] shows differentiation in experimental bulk systems; extension to LSC depletion [S1] or elimination of resistant cells [S2] is conjecture to be tested, not assumed.
5. Context bridge: applicability across genotypes (for example TP53-mutant or NPM1-mutant disease) is provisionally assumed.

Alternative explanations.
- Pyrimidine starvation could simply kill proliferative blasts, with marker changes representing secondary, incomplete differentiation rather than a true program switch.
- The active metabolite reportedly has off-target kinase inhibition at higher concentrations (recalled, unverified), which could explain any nonrescuable effect.
- In stromal co-culture, apparent activity might arise from effects on microenvironmental cells.
- Activity could resemble venetoclax-like respiratory-chain disruption [S3] rather than DHODH enzymology; uridine rescue distinguishes these.
- Apparent differentiation might reflect selection of naturally differentiating subclones or culture artifacts.

Discriminating preclinical validation strategy.
- Panels: at least 20 primary AML specimens across genotypes, matched normal CD34+ hematopoietic progenitors, and an ex vivo cytarabine-resistant residual model.
- Exposure: dose-response of teriflunomide and its active metabolite against measured free concentrations; de novo pyrimidine-synthesis blockade by isotope tracing; uridine and orotic-acid rescue arms; DHODH knockdown and rescue in cell lines.
- Comparators: brequinar as an on-mechanism tool compound; venetoclax with azacitidine as the metabolism-directed benchmark [S3]; cytarabine alone.
- Deliberately separated endpoints: differentiation (CD11b/CD14/CD15, morphology, maturation transcriptome); bulk apoptosis and proliferation; frequency of ROS-low quiescent LSC-enriched cells [S1]; LSC repopulating frequency by limiting-dilution xenograft before and after treatment; metabolic phenotype of surviving cells [S2].
- Selectivity: normal CD34+ colony-forming and long-term culture-initiating cell assays, protein-binding measurement, hepatotoxicity and mitochondrial-toxicity screens in normal cells as required by the evidence-boundary rules.

Falsifying observation. The drug-mechanism-context link is disconfirmed if, at verified clinically achievable free concentrations, primary AML blasts show (a) bulk apoptosis without increased myeloid differentiation markers; or (b) differentiation and growth arrest that persist despite pyrimidine repletion restoring nucleotide pools, indicating DHODH-independent off-target or general cytotoxic mechanisms; or (c) persistence of cytarabine-resistant, OxPhos-biased residual cells [S2], consistent with salvage-pathway bypass; or (d) comparable suppression of normal CD34+ proliferation and differentiation at equal concentrations, indicating no therapeutic window.

Selectivity and translational limitations.
- Protein binding and slow accumulation kinetics may prevent adequate unbound tumor exposure; this must be measured first.
- Reported class safety signals include hepatotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and rare cytopenias (recalled, unverified), plausibly limiting use in myelosuppressed patients.
- [S1], [S2], and [S4] derive from model systems; patient heterogeneity and microenvironmental effects remain unaddressed.
- Whether this or related DHODH-directed AML approaches already exist preclinically or clinically must be verified before any novelty claim; the packet is not a comprehensive review and predates 2025.
- No established AML regimen is being rebranded: venetoclax-azacitidine appears solely as comparator [S3].

Self-estimate rationale: promisingness is moderate because an approved, orally available drug and two convergent rationales (differentiation plus resistant-cell metabolism) are attractive, while exposure feasibility and unknown prior art temper confidence; these are personal judgments, not grades.

Ranked proposal:
Teriflunomide repurposing as a DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism AML

Teriflunomide, an oral dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH) inhibitor approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis, will induce genuine myeloid maturation in AML blasts and in residual disease and stem-cell-enriched compartments at concentrations achievable from its approved dosing, acting through on-target depletion of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The approval and indication are recalled, not supplied in the packet, and require verification (unverified prior knowledge). Leflunomide, recalled as a rheumatoid-arthritis prodrug yielding the same active metabolite, is the secondary formulation of the same premise, also unverified.

Biological context. The proposal targets two experimentally defined AML states from the packet: ROS-low, quiescent, BCL-2-high leukemia stem cells dependent on oxidative phosphorylation [S1], and chemotherapy-resistant residual cells that are not enriched for stem cells but require oxidative metabolism with mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features [S2]. The primary endpoint is differentiation, not nonspecific bulk killing [S4].

Supported premises.
- P1 (from S4): DHODH inhibition overcomes the differentiation blockade in experimental AML, establishing pyrimidine synthesis as a maturation switch rather than only a growth dependency.
- P2 (from S2): a therapeutically relevant residual state after cytarabine exposure is oxidative-metabolism-dependent, and altering that state changed treatment response in the studied models.
- P3 (from S1): quiescent, ROS-low leukemia stem cells define a definable compartment with quantifiable metabolic features, enabling a stem-level readout.
- P4 (comparator, from S3): venetoclax-azacitidine is the established metabolism-targeted benchmark that disrupted leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism in patients; it is used only as a benchmark and is not part of the novel claim.

Speculative bridges (explicitly hypothetical).
- B1: teriflunomide reproduces the DHODH-inhibitory, pyrimidine-depleting effect of the S4 compound at clinically achievable free concentrations in AML cells. Nothing in the packet establishes this for teriflunomide specifically; S4 explicitly warns that not every drug touching this pathway reproduces differentiation.
- B2 (biochemical recollection, unverified): DHODH feeds electrons into the ubiquinone pool near complex III; DHODH inhibition may therefore partially de-energize the oxidative residual state in S2 beyond pyrimidine depletion. This is a plausible but untested extension.
- B3: differentiation seen in bulk blasts extends to the ROS-low LSC fraction; S4 did not primarily address quiescent LSCs, and S1 cautions against assuming any mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window.
- B4 (unverified recollection): the autoimmune indication rests on activated lymphocyte dependence on de novo pyrimidines; normal hematopoietic progenitors may consequently tolerate transient DHODH inhibition, providing a therapeutic window that must be tested rather than assumed.

Alternative explanations. A CD11b/CD14 increase could reflect cytostatic stress or nonspecific toxicity rather than maturation. Effects could arise from off-target mitochondrial perturbation or stress signaling rather than pyrimidine depletion. Responses may be genotype-restricted if pyrimidine salvage capacity varies across specimens, and some samples may respond by apoptosis rather than differentiation.

Discriminating preclinical strategy.
1) Exposure anchoring: verify teriflunomide clinical pharmacokinetics from primary sources and bracket free-drug ranges; test AML cell lines (MOLM-13, HL-60, OCI-AML3) and primary specimens.
2) On-target pharmacodynamics: measure pyrimidine-pool changes such as dUMP accumulation, benchmarked against the validated DHODH inhibitor from S4 as positive control. Uridine must rescue both the metabolic and differentiation phenotypes; failure of uridine rescue falsifies the B1-mediated mechanism.
3) Differentiation endpoints: CD11b/CD14/CD15 flow cytometry, morphology, NBT reduction, and transcriptional maturation signatures, with apoptosis measured in parallel to separate maturation from killing.
4) Residual-disease arm: apply teriflunomide after cytarabine in S2-like models and quantify oxygen consumption and fatty-acid oxidation. A uridine-sensitive respiratory decline would support B2; a uridine-insensitive decline would indicate off-target mitochondrial toxicity.
5) Stem-cell arm: track the ROS-low CD34+/CD38- fraction from primary specimens as defined in S1 and measure colony-forming capacity; include venetoclax as a comparator anchored to S3.
6) Normal-cell counter-assay: cord-blood and normal CD34+ progenitor colony formation and maturation at the same concentrations to define the therapeutic window.

Falsifying observations. The drug-mechanism-context relationship is disconfirmed if (i) teriflunomide fails to produce uridine-reversible, DHODH-inhibitor-matching differentiation at concentrations achievable from approved dosing; (ii) the phenotype is reproduced by a nonspecific cytostatic agent and fails functional maturation assays; or (iii) normal progenitor colony formation is suppressed below the concentration needed for AML differentiation, eliminating the therapeutic window.

Limitations. All approval, exposure, and safety facts (recalled hepatotoxicity and embryotoxicity concerns) are unverified prior knowledge requiring primary-source confirmation. Model dependence is substantial: S1-S3 are specific specimens and settings, not universal evidence. Any prior preclinical or clinical AML evaluation of leflunomide or teriflunomide would need checking before novelty is claimed; the packet contains none. Venetoclax-azacitidine remains an established AML regimen and is used here strictly as a mechanistic comparator.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved DHODH inhibitor for relapsing multiple sclerosis, as a uridine-reversible differentiation therapy for acute myeloid leukemia

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.

TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in proliferating AML blasts.

HYPOTHESIS AND ORIGINAL INDICATION. Teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (approval and label facts: unverified prior knowledge, must be checked; leflunomide for rheumatoid arthritis is the alternative repurposed agent and, to my recollection, converts to the same active metabolite — unverified). I hypothesize that at free-drug exposures achievable in treated humans, teriflunomide depletes de novo pyrimidine pools in primary AML blasts and that this pyrimidine depletion, rather than nonspecific cytotoxicity, reactivates myeloid differentiation with a therapeutic window over normal CD34+ progenitors. Background biochemistry: DHODH performs the mitochondrial, electron-transport-coupled step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (standard biochemistry, prior knowledge). Note: venetoclax-azacitidine is cited only as a comparator; this proposal is not that established regimen and claims no regenerative novelty for it.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (packet-derived). (P1) DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation blockade in experimental AML and improved disease-related endpoints in the studied models [S4]. (P2) AML populations are metabolically heterogeneous: quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells show OXPHOS/BCL-2 dependencies [S1], while cytarabine-resistant cells are oxidative-metabolism dependent but not necessarily LSC-enriched [S2]. These define which populations the hypothesis does and does not claim to affect. (P3) A metabolism-directed drug pair already disrupts LSC energy metabolism in patients [S3], establishing that metabolism-targeting is clinically feasible and providing a benchmark.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES (explicitly unproven). (B1) Drug bridge: a different, approved DHODH inhibitor reproduces the [S4] phenotype at human plasma free-drug levels; risk of potency-versus-exposure mismatch, and high protein binding could lower free levels (binding fraction: unverified prior knowledge). (B2) Residual-disease bridge: because DHODH activity is linked to the ubiquinone/electron-transport pool, DHODH inhibition might partially restrain the oxidative metabolism that characterizes cytarabine-resistant cells [S2]; this is a testable bridge, not a premise. (B3) Population bridge: differentiating cells derive mainly from cycling blasts, whereas quiescent ROS-low LSCs [S1] are predicted to be comparatively spared, implying single-agent differentiation may not clear LSCs.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Apparent differentiation could reflect general antiproliferative stress, off-target redox or immunomodulatory effects, mitochondrial perturbation independent of pyrimidine depletion, accumulation of upstream metabolites, or sample-level differences in salvage-pyrimidine capacity that mask dependence on de novo synthesis.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY. (1) Verify label, dosing, half-life, protein binding, and toxicity of teriflunomide outside this packet, then bracket primary-AML exposures to measured or verified human free plasma concentrations. (2) Biochemical engagement: LC-MS quantification of pyrimidine pools in primary blasts with and without uridine/nucleoside rescue; an effect reversed by pyrimidine rescue, or recapitulated by the [S4] on-target inhibitor (brequinar; name = prior knowledge), supports DHODH/pyrimidine mediation. (3) Differentiation endpoints (CD11b/CD14, morphology, colony-forming decline) versus positive control [S4], vehicle, and normal CD34+ CFU-GM assays for therapeutic index. (4) NSG xenografts at human-equivalent exposures: assess cycling-fraction differentiation, marrow blast burden, and limiting-dilution LSC frequency. (5) Include a venetoclax-azacitidine benchmark arm [S3] probing LSC metabolism, to establish non-redundancy with an established comparator without repeating it as a discovery.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. The drug–mechanism–context relationship is disconfirmed if: (i) no uridine-reversible pyrimidine depletion occurs at achievable free concentrations; (ii) differentiation or toxicity persists despite pyrimidine replenishment (off-target mechanism); (iii) normal CD34+ progenitor colony formation is suppressed at equivalent exposures (no selectivity); (iv) PDX models show no CD11b/CD14 gain and no blast reduction; (v) any effect on oxidative residual-cell metabolism is not rescued by uridine, falsifying B2 as DHODH-mediated.

LIMITATIONS. Every teriflunomide-specific pharmacology fact lies outside the packet and needs verification. Prior clinical DHODH-directed attempts in AML with other inhibitors were, to my recollection, limited; check trials databases before asserting novelty, and if teriflunomide is already tested in AML, reframe this as context refinement rather than discovery. The [S4] findings are model-derived and not automatically transferable; single-agent differentiation is unlikely to eradicate quiescent LSCs [S1,S2], defining a translational gap; and genotype-dependent reliance on de novo versus salvage pyrimidine synthesis (unverified) may restrict the responsive AML context.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in proliferating AML blasts

A weeks-long half-life causes slow pharmacodynamics and delayed response assessment (label detail unverified); class risks — hepatotoxicity, myelosuppression, immunosuppression, teratogenicity — require label confirmation; per recalled numbers the exposure window is narrow, so the paper gate may terminate early; murine plasma uridine and species DHODH differences complicate xenograft translation; sub-1% free-fraction measurement error moves the threshold. Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for pyrimidine-flux-high, differentiation-blocked AML

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of proliferating AML blasts dependent on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

HYPOTHESIS, ORIGINAL INDICATION, AND QUANTITATIVE EXPOSURE PREDICTION. Teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (approval and label facts: unverified prior knowledge, must be checked). Its active metabolite A77 1726 (shared with leflunomide, also unverified) inhibits DHODH, the mitochondrial electron-transport-coupled step of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (standard biochemistry, prior knowledge). I hypothesize that at steady-state free plasma concentrations achievable under continuous oral MS dosing—provisionally estimated at ~0.01–0.1 µM free fraction based on typical total plasma levels of ~10–30 µM and ≥99% protein binding (both unverified prior knowledge requiring verification)—teriflunomide depletes de novo pyrimidine pools in primary AML blasts and reactivates myeloid differentiation with a therapeutic window over normal CD34+ progenitors. The go/no-go gate is quantitative: the free-drug concentration must exceed the measured blast DHODH IC50 (by a prespecified margin of ≥3×) while staying below the concentration suppressing normal CD34+ CFU-GM by >50%.

GENUINE INCREMENT BEYOND S4. The novel elements are threefold: (a) pharmacodynamic uniqueness—teriflunomide's chronic oral continuous dosing with a long-lived active metabolite sustains free-drung Exposure above a differentiation threshold in a way that investigational inhibitors requiring pulsed dosing cannot; (b) a defined responding subset specified by measurable baseline biomarkers (below); (c) mechanistic non-overlap with the established VEN-azacitidine axis [S3], since differentiation-inducing pyrimidine depletion targets cycling blasts rather than BCL-2-dependent OXPHOS in quiescent LSCs [S1]. Precedent check: A77 1726/leflunomide has been reported in preclinical AML models and possibly early-phase trials (my recollection: unverified; must be checked in trials databases and literature before asserting first-in-disease status). The specific increment claimed here—not merely 'another DHODH inhibitor'—is the biomarker-defined subset delineation and the continuous-exposure PK argument.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (packet-derived). P1: DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation blockade in experimental AML [S4]. P2: AML metabolic heterogeneity is established—quiescent ROS-low LSCs depend on OXPHOS/BCL-2 [S1]; cytarabine-resistant cells are oxidative-metabolism-dependent without consistent LSC enrichment [S2]. P3: Metabolism-directed therapy in AML patients is feasible [S3], providing a benchmark.

PRE-SPECIFIED RESPONSIVE-SUBSET BIOMARKER PANEL. Upfront stratification across ≥10 diverse primary AML specimens (core-binding-factor, NPM1-mutant, TP53-mutant, monosomal karyotype; de novo and relapsed) measuring: (i) baseline pyrimidine pool sizes by LC-MS; (ii) uridine-rescue sensitivity as operational proof of de novo dependency; (iii) salvage-pathway enzyme expression (uracil phosphoribosyltransferase, concentrative nucleoside transporters) by transcript and functional uptake assays. Predicted responsive subset: high baseline de novo flux, low salvage uptake capacity, uridine-rescuable pyrimidine depletion. Predicted resistant subset: high salvage capacity masking DHODH inhibition.

SPECULATIVE BRIDGES. B1: A77 1726 reproduces the S4 differentiation phenotype at human free-drug levels; risk of potency–exposure mismatch. B2: DHODH activity couples to ubiquinone/Electron-transport state; inhibition might partially restrain oxidative metabolism in cytarabine-resistant cells [S2]—testable, not premise. B3: Differentiating cells derive from cycling blasts; quiescent ROS-low LSCs [S1] predicted comparatively spared.

SAFETY GATING AND STEADY-STATE PK-PD MODEL. Before any translational step: (i) construct a physiologic steady-state PK model bridging approved oral MS dosing to predicted free plasma AUC; (ii) require that the AUC above blast DHODH IC50 exceeds the differentiation-threshold exposure in a ≥70% model-simulated patient population; (iii) predefine safety gates including hepatotoxicity (ALT/AST thresholds per label), embryo-fetal risk with mandatory accelerated-elimination procedure availability, myelosuppression monitoring, and no dose-limiting cytopenia in normal CD34+ CFU assays at target exposure. All label-dependent parameters require verification.

DISCRIMINATING PRECLINICAL TEST STRATEGY. (1) Verify teriflunomide label, dosing, half-life, protein binding, A77 1726 PK literature (outside packet). (2) Measure blast DHODH IC50 of A77 1726 in primary AML. (3) Run LC-MS pyrimidine-pool quantification ± uridine rescue across the biomarker-stratified panel, with brequinar (prior knowledge) as on-target comparator and S4-positive-control. (4) Differentiation endpoints (CD11b/CD14, morphology, CFU decline) versus controls including normal CD34+ CFU-GM for therapeutic index. (5) Biomarker-predicted responsive vs. resistant subsets tested side-by-side to validate the stratification model. (6) NSG xenografts at human-equivalent exposures: cycling fraction, CD11b/CD14 gain, blast burden, limiting-dilution LSC frequency. (7) VEN-azacitidine benchmark arm [S3] to quantify non-redundancy.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. (i) No uridine-reversible pyrimidine depletion at ≥3× blast DHODH IC50 achievable free concentration. (ii) Differentiation persists despite pyrimidine replenishment. (iii) Normal CD34+ CFU-GM suppressed >50% below target exposure. (iv) No CD11b/CD14 gain or blast reduction in PDX. (v) Biomarker-predicted responsive subset does not differ from resistant subset in differentiation output. (vi) Steady-state free AUC below the required window for ≥70% of simulated patients. (vii) Oxidative-residual-cell effects not rescued by uridine, falsifying B2.

LIMITATIONS. Every teriflunomide-specific pharmacology parameter is unverified. A77 1726 precedent in AML requires explicit literature/trial-database check; if already tested, this reframes as subset-refinement rather than novel repurposing. S4 findings are model-derived and not automatically transferable. Single-agent differentiation unlikely to eradicate quiescent LSCs [S1,S2], defining a translational gap requiring combination strategy. The estimated free-drug concentration range is an unverified hypothesis, not established fact, and serves as the primary falsification target of this proposal.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor that induces pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of proliferating AML blasts dependent on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for a flux-defined subset of differentiation-blocked AML

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. ## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor driving pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of cycling AML blasts.

HYPOTHESIS AND ORIGINAL INDICATION. Teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis at chronic daily oral dosing (approval, dose, half-life, protein binding, and all label facts: unverified prior knowledge, to be verified). Teriflunomide is the active metabolite shared with leflunomide (unverified) and inhibits DHODH, the respiratory-chain-coupled enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis (standard biochemistry: prior knowledge). Hypothesis: at steady-state free (unbound) exposures achievable under approved multiple-sclerosis dosing, teriflunomide depletes de novo pyrimidine pools in a definable subset of cycling primary AML blasts and reactivates myeloid differentiation with selectivity over normal CD34+ progenitors.

QUANTIFIED EXPOSURE BRIDGE (B1). Falsifiable prediction: steady-state total A77 1726-class plasma levels at approved dosing fall in the tens-of-micromolar range with >99% protein binding (leflunomide-era monitoring reportedly targeted total troughs of about 20 µg/mL; all unverified), implying free steady-state exposure of roughly 0.1–1 µM. Predefined go/no-go window: the blast DHODH IC50, measured in serum-supplemented primary-blast assays, must be at or below the achievable free trough; a >5–10-fold gap falsifies B1 before any animal work. Because differentiation is cell-cycle dependent, the operative variable is the sustained free trough over days; teriflunomide's long half-life and chronic dosing (unverified) are proposed to fit this, and pulse-versus-continuous experiments test rather than assume it.

NOVEL INCREMENTS (quantified, not generic). Three defined advances over a bare S4 extension: (1) approved-agent pharmacology — preexisting human steady-state PK and reversibility via accelerated-elimination procedures (unverified label), enabling de-risked discontinuation in older AML patients; (2) a DHODH-dependence score converting genotype and salvage caveats into a pre-specified patient-selection rule; (3) predicted non-overlap with the BCL-2/OXPHOS axis [S1,S3] as combination logic, without re-proposing any established regimen. Precedent gate: explicitly search literature and registries for A77 1726, leflunomide, and teriflunomide in AML models and trials; if that drug–AML–differentiation mapping already exists, the contribution is reframed as the biomarker-defined subset and combination logic, not discovery.

SUPPORTED PREMISES (packet-derived). P1: DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation blockade in experimental AML and improved disease-related endpoints [S4]. P2: metabolic heterogeneity — quiescent ROS-low leukemia stem cells are OXPHOS/BCL-2 dependent [S1] and cytarabine-resistant residual cells are oxidative-metabolism dependent without consistent LSC enrichment [S2]; the hypothesis claims differentiation of cycling blasts, explicitly not LSC eradication. P3: patient-level LSC energetics disruption is clinically feasible [S3], used only as benchmark and comparator.

RESPONSIVE-SUBSET BIOMARKER (pre-specified). Predicted responders: primary samples showing ≥50% UTP/dTTP pool depletion at ≤1 µM free-equivalent exposure, CD11b/CD14 differentiation rescued by uridine, and low effective salvage supply (low uridine/cytidine uptake, low SLC29A1/ENT1 expression; transporter names: unverified prior knowledge). Predicted non-responders: salvage-high samples in which physiologic uridine (low-micromolar plasma; unverified) rescues the de novo blockade, and quiescent ROS-low LSC-dominant compartments [S1]. The score combines LC-MS baseline pyrimidine pools, nucleoside-uptake phenotyping, uridine-rescue EC50, and Ki-67 cycling fraction across genotype- and phase-stratified primary samples (NPM1/FLT3, TP53, IDH1/2, RAS-pathway strata; AML genetics: unverified prior knowledge).

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Differentiation could reflect antiproliferative stress, off-target mitochondrial/redox effects through the shared ubiquinone pool, kinase or immunomodulatory off-targets at these exposures (unverified), dihydroorotate accumulation, culture-nucleoside artifacts, or stress-induced terminal maturation unrelated to pyrimidine depletion.

(2) Engagement: LC-MS pools plus 13C-aspartate/glutamine tracing of de novo flux, uridine rescue, brequinar recapitulation (brequinar: prior knowledge), and DHODH knockdown phenocopy with rescue. (3) Pulse versus continuous exposure: differentiation predicted only under sustained low-level exposure (teriflunomide-specific pharmacodynamic claim). (4) Stratification panel scoring the biomarker across genotypes and disease phases. (5) Selectivity: normal cord-blood CD34+ CFU-GM at equal free exposures. (6) NSG PDX at human-equivalent free exposures with a venetoclax–azacitidine benchmark arm [S3], reading marrow blast burden, cycling-fraction differentiation, and limiting-dilution LSC frequency; an optional combination arm tests orthogonality. B2 (partial restraint of oxidative residual-cell metabolism via DHODH-ubiquinone coupling [S2]) is tested separately as a bridge, not a premise.

SAFETY AND PK/PD GATING. A steady-state PK/PD model must bridge approved multiple-sclerosis dosing to the measured blast differentiation threshold; proceed only if that threshold sits at or below free exposures tolerated in the approved population. Gates: hepatic monitoring (known label hazard: unverified), embryo-fetal risk with pregnancy prevention and documented elimination capacity (unverified), and CBC/myelosuppression watch given baseline AML cytopenias.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATIONS. (i) No uridine-reversible pyrimidine depletion at ≤1 µM free exposure. (ii) Differentiation or toxicity persists despite pyrimidine replenishment or DHODH-independent rescue. (iii) Normal CD34+ colony formation suppressed at equal free exposure. (iv) PDX models show no CD11b/CD14 gain and no blast-burden reduction. (v) Any effect on residual oxidative metabolism is uridine-irreversible, refuting B2. (vi) Differentiation is reversed by physiologic plasma uridine. (vii) Required free exposure exceeds the tolerated PK/PD window. (viii) The precedent search finds established A77 1726–AML differentiation work, forcing the pre-specified reframing.

LIMITATIONS. Every teriflunomide pharmacology fact lies outside this packet; the 0.1–1 µM free-exposure estimate is a labeled hypothesis, not verified data. [S4] is model-derived and transfer is unproven; single-agent differentiation will not address quiescent LSCs [S1,S2], leaving a combination-dependent translational gap. [S3] is not randomized comparative evidence. Salvage-pathway determinants and AML genomics used as stratifiers require verification, and the biomarker is hypothesis-generating rather than validated.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, as a DHODH inhibitor driving pyrimidine-depletion-dependent myeloid differentiation in a biomarker-defined subset of cycling AML blasts.

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.
