HYPOTHESIS TITLE: Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for a flux-defined subset of differentiation-blocked AML.

CORE HYPOTHESIS AND CONTEXT. Teriflunomide (original indication: relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis; indication and monitoring details to be confirmed against the FDA/EMA label) inhibits DHODH in AML blasts at free concentrations achievable on routine outpatient dosing. DHODH block depletes de novo pyrimidine synthesis, releases the myeloid differentiation block, and drives terminal maturation with cell-cycle exit — the mechanistic core is [S4]. The claim is restricted to a flux-defined context: CD11b/CD14-low blasts with a high baseline dihydroorotate:orotate (DHO:orotate) ratio, high de novo pyrimidine flux, and limited uridine-salvage capacity. It is not a stem-cell-eradication claim, and teriflunomide is not an established AML regimen.

Step 0 (administrative, before any live-cell work): verify the label steady-state exposure and free fraction and class DHODH IC50 values from primary pharmacology sources. Working anchors, revised and still unverified prior knowledge: mean steady-state total teriflunomide at 14 mg/day ≈ 230 µM (label value near 70 µg/mL), >99% protein-bound, giving free ≈ 1.5–2 µM; class DHODH IC50 range ≈ 0.5–6 µM, assay-dependent. Gate: in primary blasts, the EC50 for DHO:orotate shift and for differentiation must be ≤ verified free steady-state exposure with ≥2-fold margin, measured against directly determined free drug (equilibrium-dialysis or ultrafiltration LC-MS, not arithmetic from percent binding). P1 ([S4]): DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML; [S4] does not establish that any approved drug on this pathway achieves adequate exposure or selectivity — that gap is the test. P2 ([S2], precision reading): cytarabine-persistent AML cells were not enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells, and their targetable biology was an oxidative-metabolism state, not an LSC identity; this cautions against equating residual disease with the ROS-low LSCs of [S1]. P3 ([S1]): ROS-low quiescent LSCs carried BCL-2/OXPHOS liabilities — selectivity precedent only; no DHODH-on-LSC prediction is made. P4 ([S3]): venetoclax–azacitidine supplies the metabolic comparator and biomarker template; repeating it is not proposed. Genotype exemplars for screening (NPM1-mutant, KMT2A-rearranged blasts as predicted flux-high, immature responders) are analogy-based predictions, not packet-supported evidence.

NOVELTY, RE-SCOPED. Prior art limits breadth: brequinar entered early-phase AML trials with myelosuppression, and clinical-stage DHODH inhibitors are in development (both unverified prior knowledge to confirm before scoring). The primary falsifiable novelty claim is therefore responder biology: the DHO:orotate/salvage-capacity stratifier predicting responders versus non-responders inside a defined context. A head-to-head arm against a clinical-stage DHODH inhibitor at equated DHODH engagement tests whether an approved oral outpatient drug adds value beyond the class. Contingencies: if prior art already covers flux stratification, or the DHO:orotate biomarker proves assay-unstable, the novelty claim re-scopes to a functional salvage-capacity phenotype (uridine-rescue profile) as the stratifier. Final scoring is provisional pending prior-art and label verification.

SELECTIVITY (measured, not assumed). Proliferating normal CD34+ cells also use de novo pyrimidine synthesis, and clinical DHODH inhibition is expected to cause cytopenias (unverified prior knowledge). Compare baseline flux, salvage capacity, and cycling (EdU/Ki-67) between blasts and normal CD34+ cells; run normal CFU-GM/BFU-E assays at identical free concentrations. Uridine co-administration is prospectively evaluated as a normal-cell rescue lever.

B3 (demoted): DHODH donates electrons to the CoQ/respiratory chain, but no packet source links the [S2] residual oxidative state to DHODH flux; before any combination work, this needs a dedicated test — respirometry (oxygen consumption, reserve capacity) in cytarabine-persistent cells ± DHODH inhibition. B4: differentiation may impair leukemia-stem-cell self-renewal without direct killing; if not, teriflunomide is an add-on.

ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS. Off-target tyrosine-kinase actions of this drug class at higher concentrations (unverified prior knowledge); nonspecific nucleotide depletion causing cytostasis, apoptosis, or marker drift rather than maturation; electron-flux effects independent of pyrimidine starvation; culture artifacts from serum pyrimidine content.

(1) Engagement: LC-MS DHO:orotate, UTP/CTP pools in primary blasts per genotype at free-fraction-matched concentrations; thresholds ≥2-fold DHO:orotate rise and ≥40% UTP/CTP decline. (2) Specificity matrix: uridine rescues both metabolic and differentiative effects; DHODH overexpression or an inhibitor-resistant variant confers resistance; a structurally unrelated DHODH inhibitor phenocopies; failed rescue indicates off-target action. (3) Endpoint separation: CD11b/CD14/CD16 and NBT reduction quantified separately from S-phase exit and apoptosis against a cytotoxic control. (4) Head-to-head versus the clinical-stage DHODH inhibitor through (1)–(3) at matched free concentrations and matched engagement. (5) Selectivity margin as above. (6) In vivo: NSG/PDX models dosed to human-equivalent free exposure, measuring marrow differentiation, DHO:orotate accumulation, and survival, using [S3] as the analytic template.

FALSIFYING OBSERVATION. At pre-registered, directly measured free concentrations: (a) blast EC50 exceeds verified achievable free exposure; (b) engagement without differentiation (only cytostasis/apoptosis); (c) differentiative effects neither rescued by pyrimidines nor modified by DHODH genetic state; (d) normal CD34+ colony inhibition above the 20–30% margin at differentiating concentrations; (e) the clinical-stage DHODH inhibitor matches teriflunomide at equated engagement, erasing the repurposing increment. Any of (a)–(e) across the panel and in vivo disproves the drug–mechanism–context relationship.

LIMITATIONS. Slow pharmacodynamics and delayed response assessment (label detail unverified); class risks of immunosuppression, myelosuppression, hepatotoxicity, and teratogenicity require label confirmation; murine xenografts model human pyrimidine salvage poorly; DHO:orotate assay stability must be validated; all numeric anchors and prior AML DHODH-inhibitor data are recalled, not source-verified from this packet, and are stated precisely so verification can correct them before any go/no-go decision.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing teriflunomide, an approved multiple sclerosis drug, as an on-target DHODH-directed differentiation therapy for a flux-defined subset of differentiation-blocked AML

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

Hypothesis and premises. In cytarabine-residual AML with persistent differentiation blockade, insufficient adaptive uridine-salvage capacity relative to contemporaneous pyrimidine demand permits human-compatible teriflunomide exposure to induce DHODH-dependent, durable maturation and reduce leukemia-propagating frequency. Normal-cell sparing is conditional on adequate salvage reserve, not presumed. DHODH inhibition promoted experimental AML differentiation [S4]; studied cytarabine-residual cells displayed oxidative features without consistent stem-cell enrichment [S2]. Analyze these separately from the ROS-low, BCL-2-associated stem-cell population studied in [S1]. Oxidative metabolism alone is not the proposed sensitivity determinant. Venetoclax–azacitidine is an established comparator [S3], not the repurposing proposal.

Drug and exposure gaps. Unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis, inhibits DHODH, and transporter/UCK-mediated uridine salvage bypasses de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The packet supplies no verifying drug-specific evidence. Require regulatory-label, biochemical, and clinical pharmacokinetic/binding verification before efficacy testing. Establish a numerical licensed-dose unbound concentration–time envelope, including peak, trough, AUC and duration. Measure dilution-controlled marrow/plasma uridine and reproduce its observed range, including the upper end, in protein-containing stromal cocultures. Directly measure free drug in cultures and xenografts; do not escalate above the envelope. Human-compatible engagement, differentiation and therapeutic selectivity remain speculative bridges.

Adaptive biomarker. Acute incorporation alone cannot establish salvage capacity, and pretreatment demand may change. In parallel aliquots, measure isotope-resolved salvage flux under calibrated reference-DHODH blockade across measured marrow-uridine concentrations and early/adaptive intervals before maturation. Validate reserve estimates using nucleotide-pool mass balance and transporter/UCK perturbations. Estimate C(t), maximal sustainable salvage flux at each uridine concentration, and D(t), contemporaneous demand from macromolecular incorporation, irreversible losses and pool balance, in matching per-cell-time units. Sustained R(t)=C(t)/D(t)<1 is provisional; validate independently and analyze R continuously. After residual selection, inducibly increase or decrease verified limiting transport/UCK activity. Require reciprocal sensitivity shifts at matched free exposure and engagement, accounting for changing demand and drug-free growth effects.

Novelty boundary. DHODH-driven differentiation is established [S4]; salvage bypass alone is not a discovery. Prior teriflunomide/leflunomide–AML and salvage-resistance literature requires checking. The proposed increment is response prediction by adaptive R beyond baseline uptake, UCK expression, cycling and respiration. Test this in held-out paired pretreatment/residual samples, including an R-by-residual-state interaction rather than assuming residual-specific sensitivity. Failure to improve prediction negates the biomarker advantage; drug-specific novelty remains unresolved.

Discriminating tests. Include vehicle, a characterized DHODH inhibitor, genetic DHODH suppression, and venetoclax–azacitidine. Confirm engagement and pyrimidine depletion before maturation or apoptosis. Track index-sorted, initially immature single-cell lineages and confirm leukemic genotype in mature descendants; assess post-washout morphology/immunophenotyping separately from killing, viable yield and colonies. Randomized, blinded xenograft studies should quantify secondary-transplant limiting-dilution frequency after verified washout with equal viable malignant-cell doses across groups, reporting total killing separately. Uridine rescue initiated simultaneously with drug must isotope-confirm prevention of depletion without changing exposure or engagement. Supraphysiological rescue tests mechanism, not physiological protection. Delayed rescue tests reversibility: persistent maturation after commitment does not falsify pyrimidine-dependent initiation.

Selectivity gap. Normal-cell toxicity assays alone cannot establish salvage-mediated selectivity. Quantify adaptive R, cycling and DHODH engagement in normal CD34-positive subsets under identical free exposure. Use cycling-matched comparisons and bidirectional reserve perturbations in normal and malignant cells; measure normal colonies and engraftment. Attribute sparing to salvage only if reserve-dependent response persists after accounting for demand and engagement differences.

Falsification and limitations. Off-target toxicity, cytostasis and selection of pre-existing mature cells are alternative explanations. Reproducible absence of durable lineage-proven maturation or reduced propagating frequency, despite engagement and sustained depletion at permitted exposure in validated low-R residual AML, refutes the central prediction. Response despite prevention of depletion from treatment onset contradicts the mechanism; absent reciprocal reserve effects rejects salvage adequacy as the determinant. Inadequate engagement within the envelope rejects translational feasibility, not DHODH biology. Dynamic demand, physiological uridine, AML heterogeneity, marrow pharmacokinetics and progenitor toxicity may erase the therapeutic window. Clinical benefit is unestablished.

Ranked proposal:
Low uridine salvage sensitizes cytarabine-residual AML to teriflunomide-induced differentiation

At exposure compatible with verified human pharmacokinetics, teriflunomide will inhibit DHODH and deplete pyrimidines in oxidative, cytarabine-residual AML lacking compensatory salvage capacity, inducing clonal differentiation and durable loss of leukemia propagation while relatively sparing normal progenitors. Its recalled original indication is relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis; approval, DHODH pharmacology, uridine bypass, and UCK2 salvage activity are unverified prior knowledge requiring checking. Residual cells are not automatically ROS-low stem cells [S1,S2]; venetoclax–azacitidine is an established comparator [S3].

Use paired untreated/residual populations and lock high ATP-linked respiration per viable leukemic cell at the untreated reference panel’s 75th percentile. Under uridine concentrations spanning measured marrow values, assess six-hour isotope flux during standardized genetic DHODH repression before teriflunomide testing. Provisionally define low capacity as salvage-derived UTP/CTP synthesis below 30% of prechallenge total synthesis; adequate capacity exceeds 60%. Measure absolute flux, precursor enrichment, nucleotide pools, repression, and viability. Analyze intermediate donors continuously. ## Research question

Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, relieves differentiation blockade in human AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at exposures separable from venetoclax–azacitidine oxidative-phosphorylation suppression.

Biological context and hypothesis. In primary human AML that retains a myeloid differentiation block, teriflunomide will induce cell-intrinsic myeloid maturation by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH), at free concentrations compatible with its existing clinical use, with measurable preservation of normal hematopoietic colony formation. Differentiation of bulk blasts, reduction of leukemia-initiating activity, effects on ROS-low quiescent leukemia stem cells, and effects on cytarabine-residual oxidative cells are separate endpoints.

Supported premises. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models studied, linking this metabolic step to relief of differentiation blockade rather than to nonspecific killing alone. [S4] does not show that an approved drug acting on the pathway reproduces that result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity. [S1] reports that functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S3] connects venetoclax–azacitidine, an established regimen, to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation changes in leukemia stem cells; that combination is a mechanistic comparator, and repeating it is not the proposed discovery. [S2] reports that cytarabine-residual cells in the studied models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells and instead showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, so residual disease and the ROS-low population are tested as distinct contexts.

Speculative bridges, labeled as such. Unverified prior knowledge requiring source checking: teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis; it is the active metabolite of leflunomide, which is approved for rheumatoid arthritis; both are described as DHODH inhibitors; and downstream pyrimidine supplementation, commonly with uridine, is used to bypass a DHODH block. None of the approval status, original indication, target assignment, protein binding, or achievable free exposure is established by [S1]–[S4]. The first speculative bridge is that multiple-sclerosis-compatible exposure inhibits DHODH inside AML blasts enough to recapitulate the differentiation phenotype in [S4]. The second is that this maturation is dissociable from selective loss of ROS-low, BCL-2-high leukemia stem cells [S1] and from the oxidative residual state after cytarabine [S2]. The third is that a uridine-rescue experiment can assign the phenotype to DHODH rather than to off-target mitochondrial suppression of the kind associated with venetoclax–azacitidine [S3].

Alternative explanations. An apparent increase in mature myeloid cells could reflect selective death of immature blasts with persistence of already mature cells. Nucleotide depletion could slow proliferation without lineage maturation. Off-target mitochondrial or kinase effects could reproduce oxidative-phosphorylation stress [S1], [S3] or exploit the oxidative dependence in [S2]. A host immunomodulatory action related to the autoimmune indication could slow disease in vivo without blast-intrinsic DHODH inhibition. Each alternative can look like benefit while breaking the proposed drug–target–differentiation link.

Discriminating preclinical test. In paired primary AML blasts and normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells, and in separately isolated ROS-low fractions [S1] and cytarabine-residual fractions [S2], compare teriflunomide with vehicle, with an experimental DHODH-inhibitor control motivated by [S4], and with venetoclax–azacitidine [S3]. Measure morphology, myeloid surface markers, viability, cell cycle, oxygen consumption, colony formation, and limited leukemia-initiating capacity. Confirm biochemical DHODH pathway suppression in the same samples. The on-target criterion is reversal of the AML differentiation and growth effects by exogenous uridine, pending verification of that rescue metabolite. The selectivity criterion is retained normal progenitor colony formation at concentrations that differentiate AML blasts. Record bulk, ROS-low, and cytarabine-residual endpoints separately.

Falsifying observation. The hypothesis is falsified if concentrations that suppress DHODH activity in the assayed blasts produce no increase in myeloid differentiation relative to vehicle; if uridine restores pathway metabolites yet differentiation still occurs; or if normal CD34-positive colony formation falls at or below the AML differentiation concentration. A phenotype limited to loss of viability in ROS-low cells, reduced oxidative phosphorylation, and resistance to uridine rescue would reassign the effect to the BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation comparator [S1], [S3].

Limitations. [S4] is restricted to the models investigated and does not certify clinical exposure, genetic breadth, or safety. [S1]–[S3] supply context and comparators and do not transfer efficacy to teriflunomide. Human free-drug exposure in marrow is unverified and may sit below the differentiation threshold. Differentiation can transiently enlarge recognizable myeloid bulk, and blasts that bypass pyrimidine depletion or lack a differentiation block can fail this strategy. Any interaction with cytarabine is untested. Venetoclax, azacitidine, and cytarabine are not claimed as repurposing discoveries.

Ranked proposal:
Teriflunomide, an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, relieves differentiation blockade in human AML through on-target DHODH inhibition at exposures separable from venetoclax–azacitidine oxidative-phosphorylation suppression.

Qualifying blasts show CD34 or CD117 on at least 20 percent of the blast gate, CD11b below 15 percent, CD14 below 15 percent, and fewer than 10 percent of cells past the promyelocyte or promonocyte on a 200-cell differential. Unverified prior knowledge, absent from this packet and requiring label and pharmacokinetic confirmation, is that teriflunomide is approved for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and that its principal target is DHODH, the enzyme oxidizing dihydroorotate in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. On-target loss of de novo pyrimidine synthesis is sufficient to reproduce the [S4] differentiation result. This stratum matures with a wider margin than normal hematopoietic progenitors. Alternative accounts stay open. Nucleotide-stress death can shift markers and mimic maturation. Maturation is scored at 48 and 96 hours, and a time point counts only while annexin-V positivity remains within 10 percentage points of vehicle. [S4] withholds transfer to every approved pathway drug and withholds exposure and selectivity claims.

Equilibrium dialysis measures free fraction in that matrix and in xenograft plasma, and the nominal amount is set so measured free drug remains at or below the documented unbound approved-dose ceiling. Engagement is read only at 6–24 hours: at least a twofold dihydroorotate rise and at least 30 percent loss of uridine and cytidine nucleotides. Maturation is read only at 96 hours, and only while annexin-V positivity stays within 10 percentage points of vehicle. Guanosine at 100 micromolar must leave those nucleotides at least 30 percent below vehicle and cut that gain by less than half.

Brequinar is the DHODH-positive control at the lowest concentration that meets the dihydroorotate and pyrimidine criteria; its use in the [S4] models is unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide at exposures used for multiple sclerosis induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation in differentiation-blocked acute myeloid leukemia blasts, separable from BCL-2-linked oxidative phosphorylation suppression

AML contains biologically distinct compartments whose metabolic dependencies should be specified before a drug is repurposed. In the specimens studied by Lagadinou and colleagues, functionally defined leukemia stem cells often showed low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and impaired those quiescent cells [S1]. That finding motivates selective dependency studies. It does not establish an acceptable window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor. Residual cells after cytarabine were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is an established regimen linked to leukemia-stem-cell energy-metabolism changes, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, and is used here only as a comparator [S3]. Independently, DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in those models [S4]. Cytarabine-residual AML can depend on oxidative metabolism while remaining distinct from that stem-cell population [S2]. Venetoclax with azacitidine is an existing clinical metabolic strategy, so repeating it is outside this proposal [S3].

The speculative bridge uses unverified prior knowledge that must be checked against current product labels and pharmacokinetic sources. Supported premises (from the packet). (1) [S2] establishes the disease state: cytarabine-resistant residual cells required oxidative metabolism, and perturbing that state changed treatment response. (2) [S4] establishes the mechanistic precedent: DHODH inhibition overcame the differentiation block in experimental AML and affected disease-related endpoints. (4) [S3] supplies the established metabolic comparator (venetoclax-azacitidine disrupting LSC energy metabolism) used only for benchmarking arms.

Speculative bridges (explicitly assumed, untested). Bridge A (exposure): unbound teriflunomide levels achievable with approved dosing (recalled pharmacology: high protein binding, long half-life; unverified) will reach DHODH-inhibitory concentrations in marrow blasts. Bridge B (state dependence): because DHODH is electron-transport-coupled, the oxidative residual state of [S2] will show disproportionate reliance on de novo pyrimidine synthesis, giving DHODH inhibition selectivity for that state; this coupling logic is inference. Bridge C (stem-level translation): differentiation induction will reduce functional LSC frequency by limiting dilution, not merely shift surface markers. Bridge D (mechanism purity): differentiation and survival effects will be rescued by uridine, tagging pyrimidine-mediated specificity.

Alternative explanations. (1) Cytotoxic pyrimidine starvation kills bulk blasts, and apparent differentiation is skewing of surviving bulk cells. (2) Off-target biology of teriflunomide (reported kinase/proliferation effects at high concentrations; unverified prior knowledge) drives responses independently of DHODH. (3) Immune-mediated effects in vivo confound xenograft readouts. (4) Any combination benefit reflects cytarabine scheduling rather than DHODH inhibition.

(1) Engagement and specificity: treat a primary AML specimen panel, including ex vivo cytarabine-residual generation modeled on [S2], with teriflunomide across clinically relevant unbound concentrations; quantify orotate/dihydroorotate flux shifts, test uridine rescue, and include a DHODH-overexpression resistance arm. (4) Comparator arms: venetoclax-azacitidine per [S3] for metabolic-signature and LSC benchmarks, plus a potent investigational DHODH inhibitor (brequinar; unverified status) as mechanistic positive control. (5) In vivo: cytarabine-primed NSG PDX treated with oral leflunomide dosing bridged by PK to human exposure; endpoints: marrow differentiation markers, LSC frequency, and survival.

The proposed drug-mechanism-context relationship is disconfirmed if teriflunomide at unbound concentrations consistent with approved human exposure (i) fails to shift orotate/dihydroorotate flux (no target engagement); (ii) engages DHODH but fails to induce differentiation or reduce LSC frequency in the cytarabine-residual oxidative-state fractions; (iii) depletes normal CD34+ HSPCs comparably to AML cells (no therapeutic window); or (iv) produces effects that are not uridine-rescued and persist despite DHODH overexpression, indicating off-target rather than the proposed DHODH-differentiation mechanism.

Limitations. Exposure may be capped by protein binding, long half-life, and hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity warnings (all unverified prior knowledge). [S4] model endpoints may not generalize across AML genotypes; the [S2] residual state is model-derived and may not match clinical marrow; differentiation endpoints require functional LSC assays rather than marker inference; and murine pyrimidine metabolism may not recapitulate human DHODH dependence.

Ranked proposal:
Repurposing approved antirheumatic leflunomide (active metabolite teriflunomide) as a differentiation-inducing DHODH inhibitor for cytarabine-resistant, oxidative-metabolism-dependent AML residual disease

# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Teriflunomide at multiple-sclerosis-relevant exposure induces DHODH-dependent myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia blasts relative to normal CD34-positive progenitors

This hypothesis proposes that teriflunomide will drive myeloid differentiation of differentiation-arrested human AML blasts by inhibiting dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). The original indication (multiple sclerosis), approval status, the relationship of teriflunomide to leflunomide, and clinically achieved plasma concentrations are unverified prior knowledge. They require confirmation from regulatory labels and pharmacokinetic sources before they are treated as facts.

Supported premises come from the supplied summaries. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models investigated. That evidence links a metabolic enzyme to release of a differentiation block and identifies differentiation as an outcome distinct from nonspecific cell killing. [S4] leaves unresolved whether every approved drug that affects this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

The intended biological context is primary AML blasts that show morphologic and immunophenotypic differentiation arrest. Bulk viability, differentiation, and leukemia-stem-cell readouts are separate endpoints. Neighboring evidence sets the comparators. [S1] reports that functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S2] reports that residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features, and altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. [S3] connects venetoclax with azacitidine to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects. Venetoclax-azacitidine is an established comparator. This proposal uses a different drug and asks first whether differentiation occurs in differentiation-arrested blasts.

Speculative bridges. Bridge A: at exposures used for multiple sclerosis, teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in AML blasts. Drug identity and exposure remain unverified prior knowledge. Bridge B: differentiation-arrested patient blasts share the pyrimidine-linked dependency observed in the experimental systems of [S4], so this approved agent engages the same differentiation program. Bridge C: matched normal CD34-positive progenitors tolerate those concentrations with less differentiation pressure and less loss of clonogenicity than the leukemic blasts. Bridge D: the differentiation effect is separable from oxidative-phosphorylation suppression after BCL-2 inhibition [S1], [S3] and from the fatty-acid-oxidation-associated state of cytarabine-residual cells [S2]. A pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.

Alternative explanations should be tested in the same experiment. Mature-marker enrichment can follow selective death of immature blasts with persistence of a pre-existing mature fraction. If uridine salvage replenishes pyrimidines, phenotypes that appear only at high concentration may reflect off-target kinase or mitochondrial activity. Cytarabine-residual cells of the kind described in [S2] may continue to rely on oxidative metabolism whether or not blast differentiation changes. A decrease in ROS-low quiescent cells would constitute a distinct stem-cell claim aligned with the dependency class in [S1], and it would need its own positive and negative controls. AML genotype and salvage capacity are free to dominate and are unspecified here.

The discriminating preclinical test uses paired cultures of pre-specified differentiation-arrested primary AML blasts and normal CD34-positive hematopoietic cells. Teriflunomide is applied across a range anchored to verified steady-state exposure. Arms are vehicle, uridine rescue, a tool DHODH inhibitor as the class-mechanism comparator motivated by [S4], and a BCL-2 inhibitor analyzed only as the oxidative-phosphorylation and leukemia-stem-cell comparator motivated by [S1] and [S3]. Three endpoint families are scored separately: myeloid differentiation by morphology, CD11b and CD14 or other lineage-appropriate markers, and colony maturation; bulk viability and apoptosis; and, where cell numbers allow, frequency and function of ROS-low quiescent leukemia-initiating cells. A cytarabine-residual arm, built in the spirit of the models summarized by [S2], receives the same three scores so that residual oxidative disease is a separate context.

Falsifying observation: the drug-mechanism-context claim fails if exposure-anchored teriflunomide leaves AML differentiation endpoints indistinguishable from vehicle, if a differentiation increase remains after uridine rescue, or if normal CD34-positive progenitors show equal or greater differentiation or clonogenic loss at those concentrations. Failure to reduce ROS-low leukemia-initiating cells falsifies a stem-cell-eradication extension and leaves the differentiation claim dependent on the differentiation endpoints alone. Absence of activity in the cytarabine-residual arm falsifies extension to that population [S2] and limits any supported context to differentiation-arrested blasts.

Limitations. Selectivity in patients, unbound marrow exposure, and clinical benefit are unshown. Serum binding and medium uridine can distort the apparent window. [S1] withholds any assumption that mitochondrial stress implies a therapeutic index. [S2] keeps residual disease distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population. [S3] does not transfer efficacy from venetoclax-azacitidine to teriflunomide. Genotype heterogeneity is untested. Among the supplied sources, [S4] supports the DHODH-differentiation premise only; no supplied source tests teriflunomide in AML.

Ranked proposal:
Teriflunomide at multiple-sclerosis-relevant exposure induces DHODH-dependent myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia blasts relative to normal CD34-positive progenitors

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML with a differentiation block, salvage limitation under physiological pyrimidine availability, and retained oxidative metabolism, atovaquone at a verified unbound exposure is hypothesized to inhibit respiratory complex III, shrink the oxidized ubiquinone pool, and restrict DHODH long enough for fate-tracked myeloid maturation and reduced propagation. The intended mediator is pyrimidine depletion while ATP production stays largely intact. Label indications—Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, and atovaquone–proguanil for malaria—plus protein binding above 99.9% and mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge requiring confirmation before exposure claims.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells in the studied models were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a separate selectivity benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax–azacitidine is the established metabolic comparator [S3]. DHODH dependence and salvage limitation in residual cells are unshown by [S2] and [S4] and stay measured gates. Fatty-acid oxidation is accepted only from orthogonal genetic interruption and 13C-fatty-acid flux, because etomoxir-sensitive respiration is not FAO-specific.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1 is used only if titration curves separate: partial complex III inhibition may shrink oxidized ubiquinone enough to suppress DHODH before ATP loss inside verified unbound Cmax. Bridge 2: gate-positive blasts mature by longitudinal fate, while matched normal CD34-positive DHODH flux and salvage are measured in parallel so any margin is an outcome. Bridge 3: oxidative metabolism is a complex III entry point [S2], pyrimidine dependence is de novo-versus-salvage flux at physiological nucleoside levels, and [S4] is the differentiation precedent; direct atovaquone–DHODH coupling remains speculative. Oxidized-ubiquinone use by human DHODH, uridine bypass, and respiratory-chain-independent yeast URA1 are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of leflunomide (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide approved for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor.

Before any specimen campaign, Screen A confirms unbound Cmax from primary labels and titrates free atovaquone in a reference AML line for DHODH flux, ubiquinone redox, and ATP production rate. Pyrimidine-before-ATP testing continues only if a free concentration raises dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold and shifts pyrimidine flux while ATP loss stays under 20%. If those curves overlap, or that free EC50 exceeds verified unbound Cmax by an order of magnitude, the project stops, records kinetic or exposure infeasibility, and leaves specimens unopened. Screen B compares published atovaquone–AML and respiratory-chain–DHODH studies for whether residual-state timing and salvage stratification, rather than drug identity alone, are already described. This packet does not establish novelty. Overlap withdraws the novelty claim; mechanism testing continues only after Screen A passes.

Eligibility on the same specimens is a cytarabine pulse and washout, residual oxygen consumption, and FAO by genetic interruption plus 13C-fatty-acid flux, with baseline CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed cells. Salvage limitation, under physiological pyrimidine availability, means that blocking de novo synthesis leaves compensatory salvage unable to maintain UTP; substantial de novo labeling or uridine rescue alone does not establish inadequate salvage. ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and pretreatment bulk blasts are separate arms. Teriflunomide in protein-containing medium must raise dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold, hold ATP within 20% of vehicle, and lose both nucleotide and maturation effects when uridine is supplied. Maturation counts only with barcoding or equivalent longitudinal fate tracking plus absolute counts of genotype-positive immature and mature cells, showing immature cells acquiring mature markers and an absolute rise in the mature compartment rather than enrichment by selective loss. Enzyme assays must show atovaquone inhibits complex III and spares DHODH, and teriflunomide the reverse. Ubiquinone reduction and the pyrimidine-flux change must appear while ATP loss is still under 20% and before markers move; coincident ATP collapse makes that run uninterpretable. URA1, induced only after the residual state is established, must restore pyrimidines while complex III and ubiquinone inhibition remain, and both uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide or the arm stops.

Matched cycling normal CD34-positive cells are profiled for DHODH flux and salvage under the same physiological conditions. The therapeutic index is the ratio of free concentrations that meet AML maturation and clonogenic endpoints versus matched normal colony endpoints, reported as an observed result with no preset fold cutoff. It is also falsified if no free concentration lowers DHODH flux before the ATP rate, or if matched normal CD34-positive DHODH flux and salvage equal residual AML at the same free exposure.

Normal progenitors that share complex III and de novo pyrimidine dependence may erase a margin, which the index reports rather than assumes. Differentiation need not clear leukemia durably. [S2] models may differ from clinical marrow, [S4] may not hold across genotypes, and murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Exposure figures, URA1 biochemistry, and prior AML publications require external verification.

Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss

Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML with a differentiation block, inadequate salvage at physiological nucleoside levels, and retained oxidative metabolism, unbound atovaquone will inhibit complex III, shrink oxidized ubiquinone, and restrict DHODH long enough for genotype-tracked myeloid maturation and reduced propagation with ATP production largely intact. The original indication is Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, and atovaquone plus proguanil for malaria. Label wording, protein binding reported above 99.9%, and mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge pending confirmation.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a separate benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax-azacitidine is only the established comparator [S3]. Residual DHODH dependence and salvage failure are unshown by [S2] and [S4]. Etomoxir sensitivity does not prove fatty-acid oxidation, and a large de novo UTP share does not prove failed salvage.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1: ubiquinone restriction may limit DHODH before ATP-production rate falls. Bridge 2: low-salvage residual AML may mature, and parallel normal CD34-positive cells may be equally dependent. Bridge 3: oxidative metabolism supplies the complex III entry, and physiological de novo-versus-salvage flux sets pyrimidine dependence. Oxidized-ubiquinone use by human DHODH, uridine bypass, and cytosolic fumarate-linked Saccharomyces cerevisiae URA1 are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the leflunomide metabolite (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide itself for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor.

Preclinical strategy. Screen exposure before specimens. After confirming binding and pharmacokinetics, compare label-verified unbound Cmax with the free level that raises dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold in a reference AML line. Stop as exposure-limited, with no specimen work, if that free EC50 exceeds unbound Cmax by about tenfold or more; continue only if it is at or below unbound Cmax. Titrate free atovaquone there for DHODH flux, ubiquinone redox, and ATP-production rate. Adopt pyrimidine-before-ATP only if a band gives at least a twofold dihydroorotate:orotate rise and lower oxidized ubiquinone while ATP-production rate stays within 20% of vehicle. Overlap ends this mechanism. Enzyme assays must show complex III inhibition with DHODH spared for atovaquone, and the reverse for teriflunomide.

Eligible specimens receive one cytarabine pulse and washout, with CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed blasts and proliferation recorded as a covariate. Residual respiration must include an etomoxir-sensitive fraction at least 1.5-fold matched pretreatment blasts, confirmed as fatty-acid oxidation by CPT1A or HADHA disruption and 13C-fatty-acid entry into TCA intermediates. At plasma-range uridine and cytidine, failed salvage means de novo still supplies at least half of UTP and added uridine does not restore UTP under reference DHODH blockade. Teriflunomide in protein-containing medium must double dihydroorotate:orotate and increase maturation with ATP within 20% of vehicle, reversed by uridine, or that specimen stops. For atovaquone, require the ubiquinone and pyrimidine shift before maturation and with ATP-production rate within 20% of vehicle.

Track immature genotype-positive cells longitudinally by heritable barcodes or dye dilution plus immunophenotype, and record absolute mature and immature genotype-positive counts, morphology, apoptosis, and post-washout clonogenicity. Mature-marker enrichment without absolute expansion of tracked immature progeny counts as selective survival. Induce URA1 only after the residual state is set; pyrimidine restoration must leave complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact. Uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide.

Assay matched cycling normal CD34-positive cells for DHODH flux and salvage under the same physiological pyrimidines. Report the therapeutic index, with no preset pass threshold, as the free-concentration ratio of halved normal colony output versus the AML maturation and clonogenic endpoints. ROS-low stem cells [S1] and pretreatment blasts are separate arms. Xenografts then test marrow free drug, tracked differentiation, a prespecified threefold drop in limiting-dilution initiating-cell frequency, and normal hematopoietic recovery.

Published atovaquone-AML and respiratory-chain-DHODH studies must be compared for this residual-state, salvage-stratified, ubiquinone-timed mechanism. The packet does not establish novelty; overlap withdraws the proposal.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation can reflect immature-cell loss, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other targets, or ATP collapse. The claim is falsified, even with cytotoxicity, if uridine and URA1 restore pyrimidines while complex III and ubiquinone inhibition remain, yet tracked differentiation and at least a threefold clonogenic loss persist, whereas those rescues reverse teriflunomide. No separable pyrimidine-before-ATP band, or a free EC50 above label-verified unbound Cmax, also falsifies it.

Limitations. Binding may erase the unbound window and halt at the feasibility screen. Matched normal progenitors may share DHODH flux and salvage capacity. Differentiation may leave propagating leukemia. [S2] may differ from clinical marrow, and [S4] may not hold across genotypes. Murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Binding, potency, URA1 biochemistry, FAO tools, and prior studies need external verification.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.
